scenario: A man in his 50s underwent clinical assessment for a 4-month history of recurrent palpitations, fatigue, and progressive exertion dyspnea. He had no history of cardiac disease, and there was no family history of heart disease or sudden death. Physical examination revealed an irregular pulse and a systolic murmur at the heart apex. Holter monitoring and 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) recordings documented irregular narrow-QRS tachycardia in an incessant, repetitive fashion with heart rates up to 180 beats per minute and occasional short runs of wide-QRS tachycardia. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed a dilated and diffusely hypokinetic left ventricle (ejection fraction, 30%) associated with moderate to severe functional mitral regurgitation. Blood test results were within normal limits, including thyroid function, C-reactive protein, and myocardial enzymes. The patient was hospitalized, and medical therapy was initiated, including ACE inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, β-blockers, and diuretics. Coronary angiography revealed no significant coronary stenoses. A representative 12-lead ECG of the arrhythmia is shown inFigure 1.

Perform transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair
explanation: Dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia Initially, ECG recordings were interpreted as focal atrial tachycardia or paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, often observed in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy. Hence, some cardiologists suggested starting oral anticoagulant therapy and considering pulmonary vein isolation, which may be beneficial in patients with heart failure.1Moreover, based on the severe left ventricular dysfunction without apparent reversible causes and suspected nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, defibrillator implantation (primary prevention) would be reasonable if no clinical-echocardiographic improvement occurs following 3 months of optimal medical therapy.2Of note, correction of the significant functional mitral regurgitation (eg, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair) may also improve the patient’s symptoms and reduce the arrhythmia burden by reducing the hemodynamic stress on the left atrium.3 Nonetheless, careful analysis of the 12-lead ECG during the arrhythmia, focusing on the lead II rhythm strip, revealed an irregular but repetitive pattern during the arrhythmia, alternating between short and long RR intervals. Moreover, positive sinus P waves could be tracked throughout lead II at a relatively stable sinus rate of approximately 90 beats per minute (Figure 2A). These electrocardiographic features were incompatible with atrial fibrillation or atrial tachycardia (P waves < QRS complexes). Double firing over both the fast and slow nodal pathways was suspected during this arrhythmia, presenting as dual atrioventricular nodal nonreentrant tachycardia (DAVNNT).4Occasional block over the slow pathway or fast pathway occurred, observing 1:1 A:V conduction with normal or prolonged PR intervals, respectively. Nevertheless, the electrocardiographic differential diagnosis may still include repetitive junctional ectopic activity as the underlying mechanism. Of note, arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy was also suspected due to the incessant pattern of this arrhythmia with uncontrolled heart rates during Holter monitoring (arrhythmia burden, >50%).5 After obtaining patient informed consent, an electrophysiological study was performed. Multipolar diagnostic catheters were introduced through the femoral veins and positioned at the His bundle region, high right atrium, and within the coronary sinus. During the procedure under conscious sedation, short phases of stable sinus rhythm with 1:1 normal atrioventricular conduction were documented. Intracardiac recordings during arrhythmia (Figure 2B) revealed sinus atriograms (early atriograms at high right atrium), each followed by double ventricular depolarizations showing narrow QRS, normal HV interval, and physiologic His bundle activation sequence (ie, proximal to distal). These features highly suggested double nodal “firing” or DAVNNT.4Furthermore, atrial pacing confirmed the presence of dual antegrade nodal physiology, while atrial premature extrastimulation could reproducibly induce the 2:1 response (double firing), supporting the DAVNNT diagnosis. Conventional radiofrequency catheter ablation effectively eliminated the slow pathway and restored stable sinus rhythm. The patient remained asymptomatic during the successive 3-month follow-up. Holter-ECG revealed sinus rhythm without relevant arrhythmias, and the echocardiogram displayed near normalization of ejection fraction (50%) with trivial mitral regurgitation, confirming the initial diagnosis of arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.5 In summary, this case highlights the crucial role of careful, in-depth analysis of the 12-lead ECG that may dramatically impact patient management and clinical outcomes. The electrophysiological study confirmed the diagnosis of DAVNNT and guided straightforward and curative catheter ablation, avoiding unnecessary and potentially harmful therapeutic approaches such as oral anticoagulation, pulmonary vein isolation, mitral valve repair, or defibrillator implantation.

scenario: A woman in her late 60s presented to the emergency department after an episode of syncope. She described several other episodes occurring at rest over the past several weeks. She denied palpitations, chest pain, and shortness of breath. She was otherwise in excellent health and not taking any medications. She had no family history of syncope or sudden death. Her vital signs and physical examination were unremarkable. The initial electrocardiogram (ECG) results were normal, but premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) were noted on telemetry. Shortly thereafter, 2 episodes of fast polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (PVT), 30 minutes apart, were recorded, both lasting less than 4 seconds (Figure 1A). A repeat ECG showed PVCs (Figure 1B). Laboratory test results including serum potassium and magnesium as well as 3 serial troponin levels were normal. Echocardiography showed normal left ventricular systolic function without wall motion abnormalities or valvular abnormalities. Coronary angiography showed a 50% stenosis of the left circumflex artery. Instant wave-free ratio across the stenosis was 1.0.

explanation: The ECG inFigure 1B shows normal sinus rhythm with a normal axis, sinus arrhythmia, nonspecific P wave abnormality, and minor nonspecific T wave changes. There are frequent uniform PVCs with a right bundle branch block morphology and a right superior axis. Retrograde P waves following the PVCs are noted. The PVCs are superimposed on the T waves, most notably in lead aVF (the PVCs start after the peak of the T wave), consistent with the R-on-T phenomenon, with a short coupling interval of approximately 330 milliseconds. PVCs with short coupling intervals have been shown to trigger PVT and ventricular fibrillation in patients with structurally normal hearts, which can lead to syncope and sudden cardiac death. The episodes of PVT shown inFigure 1A are initiated with a PVC that has an identical morphology and coupling interval to the PVC occurring few beats earlier. The QT interval is not prolonged. There is no coved ST-segment elevation in V1through V2to suggest Brugada syndrome. No ST-segment elevation precedes runs of PVT, ruling out coronary spasm as the etiology. Provocative drug testing is not helpful since there is no suspicion of Brugada syndrome or prolonged QT interval. Options C is therapy for long QT syndrome. Option D, PVC ablation, can be a complimentary treatment, but placement of a defibrillator is required to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death. The first mention of the association of the R-on-T phenomenon with malignant ventricular arrhythmias was by Fastier and Smirk1in 1948 (Figure 2). R waves interrupting T waves were described again in 17 patients by Smirk2in 1949, with several patients dying suddenly. Two more cases of Adams-Stocks attacks due to ventricular fibrillation in patients with apparently normal hearts were reported around the same time.3,4 PVCs are ubiquitous in the general population. In the Framingham Heart Study, PVCs or more complex ventricular arrhythmias were observed in 12% of participants without coronary artery disease monitored for just 1 hour.5Initially, it was thought that the prognosis of PVCs, in the absence of evident structural heart disease, was excellent. Later, the likelihood of cardiac mortality was reportedly double in patients with ventricular ectopy followed up for 10 years.6A PVC grading system, from 0 to 5, was introduced by Lown and Wolf7in 1971. An early PVC (R-on-T PVC) was graded at 5, denoting the highest risk. Lown and Wolf referenced the earlier work by Smirk,2but the grading system was gauged to assess the risk after myocardial infarction. Grade 2 to 4 A&B per the Lown and Wolf system are frequent PVCs, multiform PVCs, ventricular couplets and 3 or more PVCs in a row. High burden of PVCs and interpolated ones have been linked to cardiomyopathy in the absence of coronary artery disease. Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation was coined to describe the arrhythmia in an otherwise normal heart and is responsible for approximately 5% to 7% of cases of aborted cardiac arrest.8Short-coupled idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (SCIVF) is diagnosed in the presence of PVCs initiating PVT and fibrillation. A review of 86 patients with SCIVF showed the mean (SD) PVC coupling interval was 293 (50.5) milliseconds and less than 300 milliseconds in 48 patients.8As is likely in this case, the majority of PVC triggers of SCIVF originate from the Purkinje system. Long-term suppression of arrhythmias with oral medications was highest with quinidine (83.3%) followed by verapamil (50%). Ablation of PVC trigger was attempted in 55.8% and was successful in the acute phase in 83.3%.8 An implanted cardioverter/defibrillator was placed. Verapamil was started for suppression of PVCs. Ablation was planned if the patient had recurrence of arrhythmias. This patient had 1 episode of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia 3 months after initial presentation; it terminated without a shock. She had no other episodes over the ensuing 5 years.

Two years prior to presentation, he had been admitted for treatment of non–ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (non-STEMI). Twenty years ago, he had a history of tachycardia because of preexcitation syndrome that was terminated with medication. On presentation to the emergency department, the patient’s temperature was 36.5 °C; heart rate, 75 beats/min; and blood pressure, 100/60 mm Hg. His initial electrocardiogram (ECG) is shown inFigure 1. The initial troponin I level was normal.

explanation: Preexcitation syndrome with de Winter ECG pattern D. Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed type A preexcitation syndrome, with obvious ST-segment depression in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave (poor skin-electrode contact in lead V2) that could not be explained by secondary ST-segment change. The findings seemed consistent with non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome (C). However, the ST-segment depression was in an upward concave pattern (not downsloping), followed by tall and positive T waves (not inverted), which are not consistent with non-STEMI. The aforementioned characteristic features are consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes in preexcitation syndrome and primary ST-T changes in de Winter ECG pattern, which is widely recognized as signifying acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion.1These ECG changes warranted consideration of emergent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as STEMI equivalent (D). Coronary angiography revealed 100% obstruction of the proximal to mid LAD coronary artery. After PCI with stent implantation, the patient’s symptoms disappeared, with a thrombolysis in MI flow grade of 3. The postprocedure ECG (Figure 2) showed that the QRS morphology was identical to that recorded during the initial ECG but with disappearance of the depressed ST-segment and tall T waves, suggesting that an acute STEMI had not occurred. Paradoxically, preexcitation was not present in the sixth beat, which showed abnormal Q waves in leads V1through V3and ST-segment elevation in leads V1through V5. These ECG changes indicated an acute, extensive anterior wall STEMI. The de Winter ECG pattern, which is highly predictive for acute occlusion of the proximal LAD, has been observed in 2% of cases with LAD occlusions.1,2This ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and symmetrically peaked T waves in leads V1through V4(or V6). The clinical implications are equivalent to new ST-segment elevation with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.1-4It implies the need for urgent coronary angiography with the possibility of PCI to avoid progression to acute MI. However, STEMI may also occur before PCI, as in the present case. Interesting findings include, first, that the diagnosis of de Winter ECG pattern was not impeded by the presence of preexcitation syndrome in the initial ECG, which can provide important diagnostic clues. Second, without symptoms, the postprocedure ECG seemed that the patient did not have an acute MI, which was actually masked by preexcitation syndrome (but unmasked in a single, non-preexcited beat). In patients with preexcitation syndrome, the positive delta wave may mask the necrotic Q wave and secondary ST-T wave may influence ischemia-induced ST-T change.5,6However, this case emphasizes that the presence of preexcitation syndrome may not conceal the changes of the de Winter ECG pattern. The ECG features in patients with type A preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern may be consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes and primary ST-T changes. Namely, ST-segment depression is in an upward concave pattern followed by tall and positive T waves in leads V1through V4(and V6). Both preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern have ST-segment depression that is in a downsloping pattern with flat or inverted T waves in the former and an upsloping pattern with tall and positive T waves in the latter. Persisting chest pain can provide additional important information for diagnosis. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of intermittent loss of preexcitation in preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern. These ECG changes indicated the presence of an acute extensive anterior wall STEMI, providing evidence for need of further treatment. The repeat troponin I level was 4.57 ng/mL (reference, <0.028 ng/mL) 8 hours after the procedure. Repeat ECG 34 hours after PCI showed intermittent loss of preexcitation, and the ST-segment elevation and abnormal Q waves were identical to that recorded in the sixth beat in the postprocedure ECG, verifying that an acute STEMI had occurred. Routine postprocedural therapy was performed after PCI. The patient was discharged home with routine management following PCI in the setting of STEMI, and he also was referred to a cardiac rehabilitation program.

scenario: A man in his early 20s presented with suspected syncope and shaking with no significant medical history. The patient fell asleep and his girlfriend tried to wake him, but he started shaking and slumped over on the ground. He denied confusion afterward but did not feel well with nausea, flushing, chest tightness, and a rapid heart rate. About 10 minutes later, he had a second syncopal episode for 2 to 3 minutes with more than 20 muscle jerks. On presentation at the emergency department, he was afebrile, blood pressure was 120/59 mm Hg, heart rate was 85 beats per min, respiratory rate was 16 breaths per min, and oxygen saturation was 96% on room air. His cardiac examination revealed normal heart sounds with no murmurs. The electrocardiogram (ECG) was performed early on arrival in the emergency department (Figure). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed an ejection fraction of 54%, mild right ventricular (RV) dilation (RV diameter, 4.1 cm), and no significant valvular abnormalities. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed no RV abnormalities and qualitatively normal RV function. Neurology consultation was obtained with concern for an epileptic seizure event surrounding the recurrent syncopal episodes. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalogram  were obtained, both of which results were normal. On further questioning, patient reported having a second cousin with sudden cardiac death of uncertain etiology in his early 20s.
explanation: Brugada type 1 syndrome with unexplained syncope The key to the correct diagnosis in this case was the ECG that was consistent with spontaneous Brugada type 1 morphology with more than 2-mm coved ST-segment elevation in leads V1 and V2 (Figure). Recognition of the Brugada type 1 pattern as a potential cause of cardio-arrhythmogenic syncope is important. The incidence of the Brugada type 1 ECG pattern in the US is thought to be as low as 0.03%.1The proposed Shanghai Score System2can be used for the diagnosis of Brugada syndrome, which relies on ECG, clinical history, family history, or genetic test results. A score of more than 3.5 points is thought to be probable and/or definite Brugada. Brugada type 1 can present asymptomatically, in which case the management is observation. However, in those with symptomatic features, such as unexplained cardiac arrest or polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation arrest, nocturnal agonal respirations, atrial fibrillation/flutter in patients younger than 30 years of age, or syncope of uncertain etiology, further evaluation is needed. In patients with unexplained syncope in the setting of Brugada syndrome, ventricular fibrillation should be strongly considered. The presence of suspected arrhythmogenic syncope alone in patients with Brugada syndrome with the spontaneous type 1 electrocardiogram pattern is a class 1 indication for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD).3An electrophysiology study for risk stratification prior to ICD placement, however, is a class 2B recommendation and is controversial. For those with symptomatic refractory Brugada syndrome or repeated ICD shocks, there is a role for epicardial ablation. During our initial evaluation, we felt seizures were lower in the differential diagnosis, however, a striking feature was his persistent muscle jerks, making convulsive syncope less likely. We felt the margin of error was quite small and the patient ultimately decided to undergo transvenous ICD placement. The decision to offer an ICD is not one to take lightly. The incidence of at least 1 inappropriate ICD shock from an ICD has been reported as high as 6.6% during a median follow-up of 2 years.4There is also the obstacle of generator changes in a young patient, which can be necessary anywhere from 5 to 10 years depending on the manufacturer used. There is also the decision of whether or not to pursue a subcutaneous ICD system when there is no indication for pacing, which has largely been shown to be noninferior to the transvenous system,5and this choice is largely driven by patient preference. As such, it is very prudent to have a systematic approach, which is largely guideline driven when offering ICDs to patients, and this played a large role in our decision to pursue such an extensive medical workup to validate the uncertain etiology of our patient’s syncope. The patient received a 7-day postdevice follow-up examination.  He was mending well and able to resume regular activities.

scenario: A 41-year-old immunocompromised man with aplastic anemia was admitted to the medical intensive care unit (MICU) for pancytopenia and neutropenic fevers. His thrombocytopenia and anemia required daily platelet transfusions and intermittent blood transfusions. For further treatment of his aplastic anemia, a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) line was inserted into his right upper extremity. His hospitalization was complicated by right lower extremity cellulitis and suspected fungal pneumonia, for which he was treated with vancomycin, cefepime, and isavuconazole, in addition to prophylactic atovaquone and acyclovir. After a week in the MICU, he developed oral ulcers and tender, diffuse, erythematous pseudovesicular papules, many umbilicated, on an erythematous base on the face, trunk, and all extremities (Figure 1). An infectious workup, including skin biopsies, was initiated.
explanation: Serial sectioning of the biopsy specimen revealed focal clusters of smudged bacteria extravasating from some vessels in the midreticular dermis with minimal inflammatory response, likely related to the patient’s leukopenia (Figure 2). Gram stain results were negative. Skin, blood, and sputum cultures grewStenotrophomonas maltophilia. Transthoracic echocardiogram did not show endocarditis. Viral polymerase chain reaction swab results were negative. The patient’s PICC line was removed and replaced with a peripheral intravenous line. Based on the patient’sS maltophiliasusceptibilities, treatment was initiated with cefiderocol, 2 g every 6 hours, and minocycline, 200 mg every 12 hours, in addition to linezolid for concurrent vancomycin-resistantEnterococcus faeciumbacteremia. Blood cultures were cleared ofS maltophilia1 day into treatment. Skin lesions resolved with postinflammatory hyperpigmentation by day 35. After 38 days ofS maltophilia–directed therapy, cefiderocol was stopped and minocycline was continued as prophylaxis. In the setting of persistent neutropenia, the patient’sS maltophiliaand vancomycin-resistantE faeciumbacteremia recurred approximately 1 week later. After extensive discussions with the MICU, infectious diseases, hematology/oncology, palliative care, and ethics teams, the patient elected to stop medical treatment and pursue home hospice care. S maltophiliais a multidrug-resistant opportunistic gram-negative bacterium with high morbidity and mortality in immunocompromised patients; it is currently the top pathogen in carbapenem-resistant gram-negative bacteremia and the sixth leading cause of ICU pneumonia.1,2Risk factors include ICU stays, prolonged hospitalization, mechanical ventilation, PICC lines, and broad-spectrum antibiotic exposure.3﻿S maltophilia’s biofilm formation facilitates adherence to living tissues and nonliving surfaces, evasion of immune defenses, and antibiotic resistance to β-lactams, including traditional cephalosporins and carbapenems, which often delays appropriate treatment and results in higher mortality.2,4,5 Cutaneous involvement ofS maltophiliainfection is rare with intact skin but can manifest as cellulitis, soft tissue necrosis, ecthyma gangrenosumlike lesions, mucocutaneous ulcers, or metastatic cellulitis due to hematogenous spread and puncture through mucocutaneous surfaces.6,7This case report demonstrating disseminated pseudovesicular papules, many umbilicated, on an erythematous base with a varicelliform appearance expands the literature on the morphologic descriptions of cutaneousS maltophilia. IfS maltophiliainfection is suspected, high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, 15 mg/kg/d, should be empirically started before susceptibilities return. In patients with sulphonamide allergy, minocycline or levofloxacin can be started and continued if tissue culture demonstrates sensitivities to these antibiotics.7If nonsusceptibility to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, minocycline, and levofloxacin is demonstrated, appropriate second-line agents should be started.7Combination therapy may also be considered.7AlthoughS maltophiliais typically resistant to β-lactams, such as traditional cephalosporins, cefiderocol is a novel cephalosporin that has demonstrated in vitro activity against multidrug-resistantS maltophiliadue to its siderophore-based transport into bacteria and stability against β-lactamases.4The duration of antibiotics is typically 7 to 14 days, determined by the patient’s clinical response.7Management also involves the removal of infected devices.7 The differential diagnosis for disseminated pseudovesicular papules in an immunocompromised patient includes bacterial, viral, and fungal infections. Unlike this patient’s monomorphic eruption, disseminated varicella (chickenpox) presents with lesions in various stages of development, including macules, papules, vesicles (often with central umbilication), pustules, and crusts. Histopathologically, varicella is characterized by intraepidermal and subepidermal vesicles, keratinocytes with viropathic effects, and multinucleated giant cells. Disseminated talaromycosis (formerly penicilliosis), which is endemic in Southeast Asia and southern China, presents cutaneously in 40% to 70% of immunocompromised individuals, with manifestations ranging from papules with central necrosis, to pustules, nodules, cysts, ulcers, abscesses, and Sweet syndrome–like eruptions.8,9Histopathologically, talaromycosis exhibits granulomas with filamentous hyphae or sausage-shaped yeast cells. Disseminated cryptococcosis can manifest with ulcers, palpable purpura, umbilicated papules mimicking molluscum contagiosum, and nodules.10Histopathologically, cryptococcosis features organisms with prominent mucinous capsules and variable granulomatous inflammation, depending on the patient’s immune status. Both talaromycosis and cryptococcosis may present with scattered varicelliform erythematous papules.10 This case report highlights the importance of maintaining a high index of suspicion forS maltophiliain immunocompromised patients. Early dermatologic consultation can facilitate prompt diagnosis and initiation of appropriate antibiotics.

scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the hospital with fever, joint pain, and second-degree atrioventricular block. His medical history included several years of diffuse xanthomas of the skin, peripheral hypereosinophilia, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary nodules, bilateral anterior uveitis, avascular necrosis of the wrist, and IgG κ light chain monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance. No diagnosis had been identified, and treatments had included corticosteroids and methotrexate. Physical examination revealed diffuse xanthomata most prominent in the periorbital region (Figure 1A) and multiple swollen and tender small joints in the hands and wrists. A 2 × 2-mm biopsy from the right periorbital lesion was obtained. Histopathologic features are shown inFigure 1B. There was no evidence of necrobiosis. Results ofBRAFimmunostaining were negative. κ and λ Stains by in situ hybridization showed rare scattered positively staining plasma cells. Laboratory studies demonstrated an absolute eosinophil count of 3180 cells/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001; reference range, 0-400 cells/μL) and normal lipid panel results; testing results for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative, and serum angiotensin-converting enzyme level was normal. Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) showed lucencies in the right parietal bone and fluorodeoxyglucose avidity of the right iliac bone, bone marrow, spleen, cutaneous and subcutaneous nodules, and multiple axillary, thoracic, and pelvic lymph nodes. Biopsies of the bone marrow and a subcarinal lymph node demonstrated aKRASG12D gene alteration.
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed diffuse infiltration of the dermis by CD68 immunostaining–positive foamy histiocytes (Figure 2). Results of additional immunostaining were positive for CD163 and factor 13a and negative for CD1a and S100 in the lesional cells. The patient had recently started treatment with low-dose cobimetinib, a reverse inhibitor of mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) kinase 1 (MEK1) and MEK2 proteins in the MAPK pathway. Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is a rare, systemic non-Langerhans histiocytic disorder commonly manifesting with multifocal sclerotic long bone lesions with sheets of foamy histiocytes seen on biopsy of osseous and extra-osseous tissues. Since its first description in 1930, approximately 1500 cases have been reported in the literature.1ECD most often affects adults in the fifth decade of life and demonstrates a 3:1 male predominance. Xanthelasma, typically involving the eyelids or periorbital spaces, is among the most frequent cutaneous manifestations of ECD; papulonodular lesions affecting the legs, back, or trunk may also be observed. Cardiac involvement has been reported in 40% to 75% of patients2and may include right atrioventricular sulcus infiltration, pseudotumor, or pericardial disease. Other systemic involvement may include the lungs, kidneys, and central nervous system, though nearly any organ system can be involved. Characteristic histopathological features of ECD include foamy histiocytes with small nuclei and surrounding fibrosis, multinucleated giant cells, and Touton giant cells, though a variety of features within the xanthogranuloma family can be seen.3ECD histiocytes are positive for CD68, CD163, and factor XIIIa and negative for CD1a, corresponding to non-Langerhans cell type histiocytosis.1Most cutaneous involvement in ECD is nodular and diffuse with foamy histiocytes and, in some cases, shows subtle interstitial-perivascular histiocytic infiltration with variable cytologic features.4Ki-67 levels are typically low in most tissue histiocytes, consistent with a slowly progressive proliferative mechanism. Although sarcoidosis can cause cutaneous lesions that may resemble xanthomas, histopathology typically demonstrates epithelioid rather than foamy histiocytes. Plane xanthomas can be diffuse or limited to specific anatomic locations, such as the eyelids, but more than half of cases are associated with an underlying lipid abnormality, which was absent in this patient; this diagnosis would also not explain the patient’s other clinical findings. Necrobiotic xanthogranuloma is a cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis that commonly affects periorbital structures and is typically associated with a paraproteinemia. This patient had a monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) but no frank hematologic or other malignant neoplasms, and skin lesions did not show histologic evidence of necrobiosis. ECD has been shown to be caused by activating somatic variants in the MAPK pathway, with most affecting theBRAFgene (specifically,BRAFV600E), while other patients demonstrate variants in theKRAS,NRAS,MAP2K1,ARAF, andMAP3K1genes. Certain phenotypic patterns have been described in association with specific activating variants, such as the skin-orbital–dominantKRAS-mutant non-Langerhans disease phenotype observed in this patient.5﻿KRASvariants can be associated with hematologic malignant neoplasms6; this patient exhibited MGUS and peripheral eosinophilia but did not meet criteria for myeloma or leukemia, and the bony lucencies on PET/CT were attributed to ECD infiltration. The appreciation of somatic variants as the drivers of ECD pathogenesis has greatly enhanced therapeutic options for patients with this rare condition. In 2017, the US Food and Drug Administration approved single-agent vemurafenib forBRAFV600E–mutant ECD based on a phase 2 trial that included 22 patients with ECD and demonstrated a 100% overall response rate by fluorodeoxyglucose-PET criteria.7Patients with ECD are now routinely treated with agents that target their specific activating variant, such as BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors. Conventional nontargeted therapies also include anakinra, cladribine, and interferons, and investigations are ongoing into blockade of other cytokines and cellular pathways.8

scenario: An otherwise healthy man in his early 70s presented to the Department of Dermatology with a 2-year history of a mildly pruritic, erythematous, and gradually enlarging lesion on the proximal portion of his left calf. The lesion had appeared without an identifiable cause, and for the previous 2 months, the patient had applied topical corticosteroids and antifungals with no improvement. Physical examination revealed an ill-defined, nonindurated, erythematous-violaceous plaque that was slightly raised but with an atrophic appearance (Figure, A). A skin biopsy was obtained for histopathology examination (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Histopathologic evaluation showed a band-like vascular proliferation in the upper dermis with no grenz zone. Vascular spaces were round and lined by a single layer of endothelial cells. No hemosiderin deposits were found with Perls Prussian blue stain. Vascular channel endothelial cells were positive for CD34 and CD31 but negative for D2-40. Based on histopathological findings, a diagnosis of poikilodermatous plaque–like hemangioma (PPH) was established. Considering the benign nature of the lesion, no treatment was performed. Poikilodermatous plaque–like hemangioma is a newly described vascular proliferation. To our knowledge, only 17 cases of PPH have been reported. It is typically located on the lower extremity of older adult men and commonly described as a slowly growing, asymptomatic, solitary, erythematous-violaceous plaque with an overlying cigarette-paper wrinkling that gives an atrophic appearance.1,2 Histologically, there is a band-like vascular proliferation in the papillary and superficial reticular dermis within a sclerotic stroma with no clear separation from the epidermis. The vessels are lined by a single layer of endothelial cells with absent mitotic activity. Vascular channel endothelial cells are positive for CD31 and CD34 but negative for D2-40. Despite its clinically atrophic appearance, epidermal acanthosis seems to be a common feature in most cases.1 Acquired elastotic hemangioma (AEH) presents as a well-delimited angiomatous plaque on sun-damaged skin with a predilection for upper extremities.3The main histopathological findings of AEH resemble those described in PPH. However, some differences exist. Characteristically, both tumors display a band-like vascular proliferation in the papillary dermis of thin-walled capillary blood vessels arranged parallel to the epidermis. While in PPH there is no clear separation between the epidermis and the band-like proliferation, in AEH, the grenz zone is present. In addition, solar elastosis is prominent and invariably present in AEH, while in PPH, there is a loss of elastic fibers. Vascular channels of both lesions are lined by a single layer of monomorphic endothelial cells without mitotic figures, but some discrepancies exist about the nature of these vascular structures in AEH.3,4The lesions are commonly positive for CD31 and CD34, but a rarely reported D2-40 positivity may suggest a lymphatic differentiation.4 Microvenular hemangioma (MH) is an uncommon acquired benign vascular neoplasm that typically presents as a solitary lesion but can be multiple or eruptive. It has been proposed that MH could represent an idiopathic reactive response rather than a neoplastic process.5Generally, MH has a predilection for the trunk, and the average age of presentation is the third decade. The clinical appearance is variable and ranges from red or violaceous plaques to flesh-colored nodules. Histologically, MH does not exhibit a band-like proliferation but a collection of thin-walled branched vessels with collapsed lumens involving the reticular dermis. Characteristically, the vessels tend to dissect through the collagen bundles.6Endothelial cells do not show signs of atypia, and immunohistochemical stains are positive for CD31, CD34, and WT-1 but negative for D2-40 and GLUT-1.7 Acroangiodermatitis, or pseudo–Kaposi sarcoma, is a reactive process usually associated with venous insufficiency or other disorders giving impaired vascular flow. It clinically presents as purple-colored, brown, or dusky patches, plaques, or nodules on the lower extremities, but the distribution of the lesions is diverse and depends on the underlying condition.8Histopathological examination shows a proliferation of newly formed thick-walled vessels lined by a single layer of endothelial cells. Extravasation of red blood cells, hemosiderin pigment deposition, and the presence of an inflammatory mononuclear infiltrate are common.9 Poikilodermatous plaque–like hemangioma is considered a benign entity, as to our knowledge no malignant transformation has been reported in the published cases. Therefore, treatment is not necessary. Further studies are needed to fully understand the nature of this newly described condition.

scenario: A woman in her 60s with previous breast carcinoma diagnosed 11 years prior, currently in complete remission, presented with pruritic lesions on her upper body. Physical examination revealed more than 10 monomorphous, 5- to 10-mm, pink papules with telangiectasias and white background on dermoscopy, distributed on the chest, arms, and back (Figure 1). There were palmoplantar keratosis and pits. The patient underwent thyroid ultrasonography, abdominal ultrasonography, colonoscopy, and central nervous system magnetic resonance imaging. These explorations revealed 1 Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS) level 5 lesion, a kidney mass, and more than 100 colonic polyps.
explanation: Shave biopsy specimens were obtained for pathologic examination (Figure 2) and revealed well-circumscribed, nonencapsulated dermal nodules with hypocellular, thickened, and homogenized eosinophilic collagen bundles arranged in a laminated manner with intervening prominent clefts. Histopathological examination findings were consistent with sclerotic fibroma or storiform collagenoma. A second nodule on the patient showed similar findings. Multiple sclerotic fibromas can be associated with Cowden syndrome (CS) or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2). Given the presence of acral pits, the patient fulfilled a pathognomonic criterion for CS according to the International Cowden Consortium diagnostic criteria. Five biopsied polyps were hamartomatous polyps. The samePTENvariation was detected in the skin and hamartomatous polyps. Furthermore, DNA analysis in peripheral blood detected aPTENmosaicism with an allelic frequency of 5.5%. CS is an autosomal dominant genodermatosis, withPTENvariations occurring in 35% of patients. It is characterized by the presence of cutaneous lesions and systemic neoplasms, either benign or malignant, such as thyroid carcinoma, breast carcinoma, colonic hamartomatous polyposis, kidney carcinoma, and dysplastic gangliocytoma of the cerebellum (Lhermitte-Duclos disease), among others. Cutaneous lesions related to CS include trichilemmomas, acral keratosis and acral pits, mucocutaneous neuromas, oral papillomas, and sclerotic fibromas.1,2Dermoscopic features of sclerotic fibromas were first reported in 2018 by Ebadian et al.3They described the presence of a white background with peripheral arborizing vessels.3This dermoscopic pattern can also be seen in atypical dermatofibromas, late stages of sclerotic dermatofibromas, and amelanotic blue nevi.3,4 MEN2 syndrome is characterized by the presence of thyroid medullary cancer, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism. Cutaneous features associated with MEN2 are sclerotic fibromas, macular amyloidosis (MEN2A), and mucosal neuromas (MEN2B). MEN2 is caused byRETvariations that interplay with the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mammalian target of rapamycin (PI3K/AKT/mTOR) pathway, wherePTENalso participates. This close association could explain the overlapping clinical findings in CS and MEN2.5 Neurofibromatosis type 1 is caused by variations in theNF1gene and also entails a higher risk for breast carcinoma. Cutaneous findings encompass cafe-au-lait macules, axillary and groin freckling, and neurofibromas.6Histologically, neurofibromas are composed of delicate cells with an oval or spindle-shaped nucleus in a light pink stroma.6-8Multiple eruptive dermatofibromas are an uncommon clinical entity characterized by the appearance of multiple dermatofibromas in a short period of time. While initially defined as the presence of 15 dermatofibromas, 5 to 8 dermatofibromas in 4 months has more recently been considered as sufficient to establish the diagnosis. It has been associated with lupus erythematosus and HIV infection, but it also has been detected in healthy individuals. Dermoscopic features of dermatofibromas are diverse, including sclerotic fibromalike features, but the most typical appearance is the presence of a central white area surrounded by a delicate pigmented network.9Clinically, dermatofibroma is typically a firm papule that dimples inward with lateral pressure. In the current patient, CS presented with subtle cutaneous lesions, which permitted the identification of the syndrome and its multidisciplinary approach.

scenario: A teenaged boy presented to the outpatient clinic with a 1-year history of asymptomatic cutaneous lesions on the face that had progressively spread to the trunk and extremities. He also had asthenia and mild intermittent arthralgias. Physical examination revealed multiple millimetric erythematous to hyperpigmented monomorphic keratotic papules involving the head, trunk, and extremities. Symmetric annular brown erythematous plaques on the cheeks and temples were also seen. There were no vesicles or pustules (Figure, A and B). Laboratory investigations revealed a normal white blood cell count, mild anemia (hemoglobin level, 11.3 g/dL; normal level 12.50-15.50 g/dL; to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0), hypocomplementemia, and moderate proteinuria. Autoimmune serology results showed raised levels of antinuclear antibodies (>1:160), anti-Smith antibodies, SSA/Ro antibodies, SSB/La antibodies, and anti-U1RNP antibodies. Anti-dsDNA antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, rheumatoid factor, IgG and IgM anticardiolipin antibody, and anti-β2 glycoprotein 1 antibody results were negative. A biopsy specimen obtained from an erythematous papule on the trunk and stained with hematoxylin-eosin is shown in theFigure, C and D.
explanation: A. Nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus Histopathological examination revealed a slightly atrophic epidermis with interface dermatitis, individual dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and a superficial perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils, admixed with numerous mononuclear histiocytoid cells. Few eosinophils and leukocytoclastic debris were apparent, but there was no evidence of subepidermal blister formation or vasculitis. Immunohistochemical study results revealed that the mononuclear histiocytoid cells showed immunoreactivity for myeloperoxidase and CD68, suggesting myeloid lineage. Direct immunofluorescence showed negative results. The presence of a prominent infiltrate of neutrophils with leukocytoclasia, as well as an interface dermatitis, supported the diagnosis of nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus (NBNLE) in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).1The patient was treated with oral prednisone and hydroxychloroquine with partial resolution of the lesions. Nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus,2,3also known as SLE-associated neutrophilic dermatosis3or Sweet-like neutrophilic dermatosis,4is a newly recognized clinicopathological variant of cutaneous lupus erythematosus characterized by the presence of a dermal and/or subcutaneous infiltrate of neutrophils and variable degrees of interface dermatitis.2,3,5The disease predominantly affects women and is clinically manifested by multiple, usually nonpruritic, urticarial papules and nodules occurring in a wide distribution.2,3Lesions most commonly develop in patients with SLE, especially in those receiving immunosuppressive therapy. However, they can also be the presenting manifestation of the disease.3Histologically, NBNLE is characterized by a perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils with prominent leukocytoclasia and variable degrees of vacuolar degeneration of the dermoepidermal junction. The neutrophilic infiltrate is usually superficial but can extend into the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue.3,6There is no evidence of vasculitis, necrobiosis, or prominent dermal edema, and direct immunofluorescence study results show complement and/or immunoglobulin deposition along the basement membrane zone in about half of cases. Exceptionally, a dermal infiltrate primarily composed of histiocyte-like immature myeloid cells has also been described.7,8The differential diagnosis of NBNLE includes other conditions associated with SLE, such as acute lupus erythematosus, Sweet syndrome, hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis, and palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis. In the rare cases of NBNLE with histiocyte-like immature myeloid cells, histiocytoid Sweet syndrome can be considered. Nonbullous neutrophilic lupus erythematosus can be distinguished from acute lupus erythematosus by its more persistent and widespread distribution of cutaneous lesions and more pronounced dermal neutrophilic infiltrate. Sweet and histiocytoid Sweet syndrome lack vacuolar degeneration of the dermoepidermal junction and show a denser infiltrate of neutrophils with prominent papillary dermal edema. Hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis show cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis, and palisaded neutrophilic and granulomatous dermatitis show variable degrees of degenerated collagen and palisaded histiocytes. The pathogenesis of NBNLE is still unknown and seems to be complex. The combination of interface dermatitis and neutrophilic infiltrates suggests that both the innate and adaptive immune system may be involved. The prognosis of NBNLE is usually good but depends on the severity of the associated SLE. Lesions usually respond promptly to systemic corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine, or dapsone.9,10In case of persistence, mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine have also been used with good response.2,3The present case highlights the wide range of clinicopathological features of cutaneous lupus erythematosus. Increased awareness of this peculiar variant is important, as it may be the first clinical manifestation of SLE.

caption: A, Large, well-defined, firm yellow to skin-colored multinodular hypertrichotic plaque on the left lower back. B, Hematoxylin-eosin staining demonstrates diffuse dermal infiltration of spindle cells, predominantly encircling terminal folliculosebaceous units (original magnification ×4). C, Higher-power magnification highlights a mix of partially fusiform melanocytes and dendritic cells with glassy, eosinophilic cytoplasm (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×40). D, Immunohistochemical staining reveals diffuse and periadnexal S100 positivity in the mid to deep dermis (original magnification ×4).
scenario: A 17-month-old boy was referred to pediatric dermatology for evaluation of a slow-growing, nontender plaque on the lower back. The child's mother reported that, on discovery, the plaque was initially 1 × 1 cm and had since grown in size with the child. She was uncertain if the plaque was present at birth. The patient’s medical history was significant for dermal melanocytosis of the right hip and mid back, increased head circumference (97th percentile), and expressive language delay. There was no family history of congenital birthmarks or neurofibromatosis type 1 or 2. Physical examination revealed a well-appearing boy with normal vital signs and Fitzpatrick type III skin type. On the left lower back, there was a 15 × 5-cm indurated skin-colored to yellow, firm, multinodular plaque with hypertrichosis, extending from the midline to the left lower flank (Figure, A). There were additional blue-gray patches on the back and right hip, as well as a small café au lait macule on the right lower back. Limited neurologic examination was within normal limits. A 4-mm punch biopsy was performed for further diagnostic evaluation (Figure, B-D).
explanation: Histopathologic evaluation findings demonstrated a diffuse dermal proliferation of partially fusiform spindled cells in the mid to deep dermis with entrapped enlarged terminal folliculosebaceous units. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for S100, CD34, and SOX-10 and negative for desmin, SMA, and CD1a. Partial expression of Melan A and epithelial membrane antigen stains were noted. This combination of clinical and histopathologic examination findings led to a diagnosis of neurocristic hamartoma. A magnetic resonance image of the lumbar spine was obtained, which showed a contrast-enhancing cutaneous lesion extending between the L3 and L5 spinal segment, with branches of enhancement extending into the paraspinous soft tissues of the L4 and the deep subcutaneous tissues of the L3 spinous process. There was no evidence of spinal involvement or dysraphism. Because the lesion extended into the deep subcutaneous tissue of the L3 to L5 spinal segments, annual magnetic resonance imaging surveillance was recommended, with a low threshold for rebiopsy if pigment or new features emerged. Neurocristic hamartomas (NCHs) are rare collections of dermal neuromesenchymal cells of neural crest origin. While NCHs were initially thought to be variants of blue nevi, they are now known to have unique clinical and histologic features.1Neurocristic hamartoma is derived from the aberrant differentiation of pluriopotent neural crest cells into Schwann cells, melanocytes, and pigmented dendritic cells.2While typically congenital, NCH may be acquired from sites of constant pluripotent-cell activation.2 Neurocristic hamartomas present similarly to blue nevi, typically as blue-to-black hyperpigmented plaques on the head or neck with focal alopecia.3While the majority of cases are seen on the scalp, NCHs have been reported to occur on the back and face.4Neurocristic hamartomas may overlap with other disorders of neural crest, including neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and neurocutaneous melanosis.2Of 32 cases of NCH reported in the literature, 12 (38%) had malignant transformation into melanoma and 6 (19%) metastasized.4-6Genetic analysis of malignant NCH has demonstrated a lack ofBRAF,GNAQ,NRAS, andKITmutations, suggesting a separate mechanism for malignant transformation compared with malignant melanoma.6Histologically, NCHs have overlapping features with blue nevi, including heavily pigmented spindled cells with a fusiform appearance and a predilection for adnexal structures.1However, NCHs have additional neural and Schwann cell differentiation.1Neurocristic hamartomas stain positive for S100, HMB-45, and CD-34 markers in the stroma.2,4 Becker nevus (BN) is a solitary hyperpigmented plaque with male predilection that may involve any region of the body. Becker nevus arises during the first decade of life, often developing hypertrichosis during the second decade of life because of its androgen-dependent nature. Becker nevus may be associated with hypoplasia or hyperplasia, or asymmetry of the affected area.7In this patient, while both BN and the NCH appeared in the first decade with hypertrichosis, BN exhibits epidermal hypermelanosis and acanthosis with few melanocytes in the dermis. Smooth muscle hamartoma (SMH) is a congenital, solitary hyperpigmented and hypertrichotic plaque commonly involving the trunk, buttocks, and lower extremities. These are distinguished from similar lesions by a positive pseudo-Darier sign. Malignant transformation has not been reported.8While both NCH and SMH can present as solitary hyperpigmented and hypertrichotic plaques, SMHs display as collections of spindled smooth muscle cells throughout the dermis, in contrast to the collection of neural crest–derived cells in NCH. Plexiform neurofibromas (PNs) are associated with NF1 and present as tender, firm subcutaneous nodules with a “bag of worms” consistency that span along the length of peripheral nerves. Superficial PNs may be characterized by hyperpigmentation and hypertrichosis, easily confused for congenital melanocytic nevi. Approximately 8% to 12% of patients with NF1 develop malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors from PNs, with the potential to infiltrate into nerves, muscle, and fascia.9Although both PNs and NCHs can demonstrate S100 positivity, the patient described herein had a diffuse proliferation of spindled cells in contrast to the clear fascicles present in PN. Neurocristic hamartoma is a rare diagnosis that should be considered on the differential for hypertrichotic plaques in children as well in cases of focal alopecia, such as aplasia cutis, especially because that is a more common clinical presentation. Owing to the paucity of reported cases, long-term management is not well understood. However, given the possibility of malignant transformation, periodic skin examinations are recommended.

caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

caption: A, Skin-colored to reddish-brown micropapules involving the neck are present. The eroded area on the right side of the neck represents a recent biopsy site. B, Dermal tumor composed of multiple small ducts lined by a twin layer of cuboidal epithelium, with occasional commalike tails, and fibrotic stroma is displayed (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
scenario: A male in his 20s presented with a widespread papular eruption. The lesions initially developed on the right side of his neck when he was 2 years old and subsequently progressed rapidly over a 3-year period, extending to the periorbital and intertriginous areas when he was aged 15 years. The lesions were mostly asymptomatic, with only occasional mild pruritus. There was no family history of similar dermatological conditions. Physical examination revealed monomorphic, skin-colored to reddish-brown micropapules involving the bilateral periorbital, neck, axillary, and inguinal regions (Figure 1A). Punch biopsies were obtained from the right side of the neck and left axilla for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathologic examination revealed dermal tumors composed of multiple small ducts lined by a twin layer of cuboidal epithelium with occasional characteristic commalike tails, with background fibrotic stroma. A diagnosis of eruptive syringoma was confirmed. At present, this patient has declined further treatment and is managing his pruritus with topical corticosteroids as required (Figure 2). Syringomas are common benign adnexal tumors that affect approximately 1% of the global population with an increased incidence in Asian and Black individuals.1,2This condition typically presents as skin-colored papules affecting the periorbital areas.1 Eruptive syringoma is a rare variant of syringoma that predominantly affects females.2In contrast to classic syringoma, the onset of eruptive syringoma typically occurs before or during puberty.3The neck is the most common site of onset for this condition, followed by the chest and abdomen.1 Differential diagnoses of eruptive syringoma include other papular dermatoses, such as lichen nitidus, Fox-Fordyce disease, Brooke-Spiegler Syndrome (BSS), and generalized basaloid follicular hamartoma syndrome (GBFHS).2Histopathologic examination is crucial in confirming the diagnosis.4The distinct histopathological features of eruptive syringoma include the presence of cystic ductal structures lined by 2 layers of epithelial cells, with characteristic comma-shaped tails. There is usually a dense fibrous stroma.2,4 Fox-Fordyce disease typically presents with persistent skin-colored papules affecting the intertriginous areas and only rarely the head and neck region.5Fox-Fordyce disease is more often seen in postpubertal young women, rather than the 2-year-old male in this case.5Histologically, Fox-Fordyce disease is characterized by perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrate and spongiosis, associated with infundibular hyperkeratosis, dilatation, and plugging.5 BSS is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by the development of trichoepitheliomas, cylindromas, and spiradenomas.6Classically, BSS presents as multiple small colored papules preferentially involving the nasolabial fold during puberty.6These papules typically represent trichoepithelioma.6Patients with BSS also can present with cylindromas on the scalp that typically present as tender skin-colored nodules.6Histologically, trichoepithelioma is characterized by nests of basaloid cells with keratin horn cysts and abortive follicular bulbar differentiation (papillary mesenchymal bodies), within a fibrotic stroma. Cylindroma consists of nests of basaloid cells with densely eosinophilic basement membranelike material.6 GBFHS is a rare subtype of basal follicular hamartomas (BFH), most commonly presenting as skin-colored papules across the face, scalp, neck, trunk, and pubic area.7GBFHS most commonly presents at birth or early childhood and may occasionally regress in adolescence.7Other associated physical findings may include alopecia, hypohidrosis, hypotrichosis, and palmoplantar pitting.7Histologically, BFH presents with discrete basaloid proliferations characteristically arranged in anastomosing columns and cords with scant or absent stroma.7 Treatment of eruptive syringomas is mainly for cosmesis. A wide variety of treatment options have been reported with limited degrees of success. These include ablative lasers (carbon dioxide or erbium), electrocautery, cryotherapy, chemical peels, topical and systemic retinoids, and oral antihistamines.1,2

caption: A, Smooth, firm, skin-colored papules on the nasal dorsum and bilateral alae. B, Superficial telangiectatic vessels, thick collagen bundles, and prominent sebaceous glands (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
scenario: A healthy 19-year-old man with Fitzpatrick skin type V presented with a 2-year history of bumps of the nose (Figure 1A). Physical examination was notable for several smooth, firm, skin-colored papules on the nasal dorsum and bilateral alae. The patient had previously been treated for moderate acne vulgaris of the face (temples, cheeks, nose, and chin), chest, and back that had since been well-controlled using tretinoin cream, 0.1%. The nasal papules persisted, despite resolution of the remainder of his acne without residual scarring. The patient was otherwise healthy without history of developmental delay, seizures, hypopigmented skin macules, or other notable cutaneous, cardiac, or neurologic lesions. A punch biopsy was obtained to guide further diagnosis and treatment.
explanation: A. Acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules Histopathologic findings were notable for stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels (Figure 1B). Prominent sebaceous glands and deep dermal fibrosis were also observed (Figure 2). The combined clinical and histopathologic findings supported a diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules. The patient was subsequently given twice-daily sirolimus petrolatum, 1%, and evaluated for treatment with carbon dioxide laser. Given his Fitzpatrick skin type and the increased associated risk of hyperpigmentation, a test spot was pursued prior to laser treatment of the entire nasal dorsum (Active FX; 125 mJ; 3% density). Pretreatment with twice-daily hydroquinone cream, 4%, and posttreatment with hydrocortisone ointment, 2.5%, was recommended to aid in reducing hyperpigmentation and facilitating the further flattening of these lesions. Treatment thus far has been limited to the bilateral nasal alae, with the patient noting flattening of the nasal papules without associated hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation. Existing literature has postulated acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules as representative of an underappreciated scarring variant of acne vulgaris that is primarily seen in the adolescent population.1,2These papules exhibit an anatomic predilection for the nose and chin and are clinically characterized by their smooth, dome-shaped appearance. The lesions are persistent and do not resolve despite successful treatment of acne with conventional modalities, such as topical retinoids, topical antibiotics, oral antibiotics, and isotretinoin. An existing case series of patients with acne-associated nasal papules from within a single institution contained a high proportion of Hispanic male patients, suggesting a possible predilection of this pathology for male patients with skin of color, especially those of Hispanic descent.3These findings were consistent with this case, given the African American background of the patient described herein. Of note, this patient did not have a history of developmental delay, seizures, Shagreen patches, or cardiac or brain tumors to raise suspicion for tuberous sclerosis. Additionally, granulomas were not appreciated on histopathology, making a diagnosis of cutaneous sarcoid unlikely. Histopathology results lacked thickened collagen bundles in the papillary dermis, which also makes white fibrous papulosis unlikely. A confirmatory diagnosis of acne-associated angiofibroma-like nasal papules is made following observation of essential histopathologic features, including stellate fibroblasts within a background of collagenous stroma extending into the deep dermis and increased thin-walled, dilated blood vessels. There are a handful of syndromic conditions that manifest with numerous facial angiofibromas and can appear histologically similar to this entity, including tuberous sclerosis complex, multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 1, and Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome. It should be noted that this entity is clinically and histopathologically indistinguishable from classic angiofibromas. As such, clinicopathological correlation is vital, as a thorough background of the patient’s history and clinical presentation will aid in contextualizing the key elements observed on histopathology. Diagnosis in the case presented was delayed as the initial shave biopsy was interpreted as verruca plana, highlighting the diagnostic subtlety and necessity for biopsy inclusive of mid and deep dermis associated with these nasal papules. For this reason, it is important to keep this entity on the differential diagnosis when evaluating patients with a history of acne or acne scarring, particularly in patients with skin of color.

caption: A, Fifth digit ulceration with raised, erythematous borders and drainage on initial dermatology visit. B, Poorly circumscribed infiltrate of atypical epithelioid cells within the dermis dissecting between collagen bundles with mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Epithelioid cells have round to oval, enlarged nuclei with vesicular chromatin, some pleomorphic, and abundant amphophilic cytoplasm.
scenario: A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).
explanation: Histopathology results revealed an atypical epithelioid proliferation with positive staining for pancytokeratin, CD34, and ERG, with patchy CD31 positivity. There was negative staining for CD68, SOX10, S100 protein, human herpesvirus 8, calponin, p63, CK7, and CK20. Notably, there was loss of INI1 expression and no bacteria (Gram stain), fungi (periodic acid–Schiff stain), or acid-fast bacilli (Fite stain) were identified. Results of pathology, immunostaining, and imaging (Figure 2) confirmed the diagnosis of classic-type epithelioid sarcoma (ES). Immunosuppressants were discontinued, and the patient was referred to a multidisciplinary sarcoma team, ultimately requiring amputation. ES is a rare soft-tissue neoplasm most commonly affecting the distal extremities of young adults, with peak incidence around the age of 35 years.1It tends to grow along tendons, fascia, and nerves, with differentiation reflected in its varied immunohistochemical findings.2Histologically, ES appears as a dermal or subcutaneous nodule composed of epithelioid and spindle cells, which may be well circumscribed or irregularly lobulated, often with central necrosis. Immunohistochemistry typically shows positive results for cytokeratin and vimentin, with approximately 50% of cases with positive staining for CD34 and 40% showing ERG immunoreactivity.3,4ES is usually negative for S100, desmin, FLI-1, and CD31, although focal CD31 cytoplasmic expression has been described.2,5The highly sensitive diagnostic feature is loss of nuclear SMARCB1/INI1 protein expression.1 Prognosis remains poor due to diagnostic delays, high local recurrence rates, and distant metastasis. Five-year survival ranges from 25% to 70%.1The proximal subtype, typically involving the trunk, pelvis, or proximal limbs, is characterized by larger, pleomorphic cells and follows a more aggressive course.1The more common classic (distal) subtype typically affects the hands and forearms and may initially be less aggressive; however, it can metastasize, and the presence of high-grade histologic features, such as mitoses, necrosis, and atypia, results in behavior resembling the proximal variant. Importantly, ES is often chemoresistant, which explains why radical surgical approaches, including amputation in this case, may be required.1 Clinically, ES initially presents as a painless, firm dermal or subcutaneous nodule. It has been associated with prior trauma and may develop superficial bleeding or necrosis that can become painful.1Rarely, ES manifests as a nonhealing, ulcerative process with raised margins, mimicking conditions like perforating granuloma annulare,Mycobacterium ulcerans, or even PG, as in a case where diagnosis was delayed for 18 years.6Distinguishing features include the histologic absence of palisading granulomas, lack of organisms, and confirmatory immunohistochemical findings. Given the ambiguous presentation of ES, accurate diagnosis requires a high level of suspicion. HFUS has successfully identified ES even when tumors were not palpable or initially missed with magnetic resonance imaging, and it is increasingly used in skin oncology to assess lesion depth and vascularization.7,8Contrary to ES, findings of HFUS for perforating granuloma annulare typically appear as a poorly defined hypoechoic band in the dermis, while active PG demonstrates a heterogeneous, edematous process.9,10When used alongside clinical assessment and dermatopathology, HFUS can help differentiate lesions and assess involvement with nearby structures. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge in distinguishing ES from mimicking ulcers and emphasizes the importance of early imaging and repeat biopsy with immunohistochemical staining to reduce morbidity and guide appropriate treatment.
