scenario: A school-aged boy presented with occasionally pruritic, generalized hyperkeratotic papules with central white spicules and comedo-like plugs that were in a linear distribution on his face, trunk, and extremities since birth. Some of the eruptions on his trunk had spontaneously resolved with developmental growth. There was nonconsanguineous marriage of his parents, and no family members had similar lesions. The patient was otherwise in good general health and without developmental delay. Physical examination showed generalized, linear hyperkeratotic papules with numerous central small filiform keratotic white spicules and brown plugs on the head, face, neck, trunk, and bilateral upper and lower extremities (Figure, A and B), including his palms and soles along Blaschko lines, accompanied with alopecia of the scalp and eyebrows. The examination of nails, mucosae, and teeth was unremarkable. No extracutaneous involvement was observed. Dermoscopic examination showed many central white spines on the face (Figure, C) and brown cores surrounded by yellow crater-like rings on the right palm. A skin biopsy specimen was taken from the hyperkeratotic papules with white spicules on his right thigh (Figure, D).

options.C: Porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus

answer: Porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus
explanation: C. Porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus Histopathological examination showed hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and parakeratotic columns within an epidermal invagination that was overlying dilated eccrine ducts and acrosyringia in a tortuous appearance. A diagnosis of porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus (PEODDN) was made. Porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus is a rare, benign eccrine hamartoma with unclear etiology, but recent work has indicated that somatic genetic mosaicism may be associated with the pathogenesis of PEODDN, considering its distribution along Blaschko lines. Somatic heterozygousGJB2variants, including p.Gly45Glu, have been reported to be associated with PEODDN.1 Porokeratotic eccrine ostial and dermal duct nevus usually appears at birth or in early childhood, although late-onset presentations have also been reported.2Clinical features of PEODDN include multiple, asymptomatic, or mildly pruritic white-to-brown papules or plaques comprising punctate pits and comedo-like plugs, with a predilection for extremities with a linear distribution along Blaschko lines.2Generalized lesions with numerous white spicules, as with this patient, are rare. Other diseases and PEODDN may coexist, such as seizures, left hemiparesis and scoliosis, deafness and developmental delay, palmoplantar keratoderma, psoriasis, hyperthyroidism and polyneuropathy, breast hypoplasia, and keratitis-ichthyosis-deafness syndrome.3Dermoscopy results reveal central white and brown keratotic plugs that are surrounded by yellow crater-like openings that correspond with the pathognomonic findings of PEODDN, including hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and parakeratotic columns overlying dilated eccrine ducts and acrosyringia.4Thinner granular layers and dyskeratotic keratinocytes in the epidermal invagination may also be found. This case needs to be distinguished from inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus, trichodysplasia spinulosa, multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis, and lichen spinulosus. Inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus is characterized by substantially pruritic, scaly, erythematous papules in a linear distribution without comedo-like plugs, and histopathology results may show alternating areas of hyperkeratosis and parakeratosis. Parakeratosis is not associated with dilated eccrine ducts and acrosyringia.4Trichodysplasia spinulosa may also present as generalized keratotic papules with white spicules and the loss of the eyebrows and eyelashes, which are similar to the facial lesions of the current patient. However, trichodysplasia spinulosa is essentially a folliculocentric infection of trichodysplasia spinulosa–associated polyoma virus that is seen almost exclusively in patients with immunosuppression, such as transplant recipients and patients with a hematologic cancer.5In histopathology results, it reveals dilated follicular infundibula that are filled with compact hyperkeratotic and parakeratotic keratin that is admixed with dyskeratotic keratinocytes that contain trichohyalin granules.5Furthermore, positive anti–simian vacuolating virus 40 large T immunostaining and polymerase chain reaction of tissues help to confirm the presence of polyoma virus.5Multiple minute digitate hyperkeratosis predominantly manifests as asymptomatic white-to-brown small nonfollicular spiky spicules that affect the trunk and extremities, while the face and palmoplantar surfaces are not affected. Its distinctive histopathology includes digitiform orthohyperkeratosis with mild acanthosis, hypergranulosis, and elongation of rete ridges; parakeratosis and epidermal invagination are less common.6Considering multiple symmetric keratotic papules with numerous spicules on the trunk and extremities, lichen spinulosus should also be considered, but it usually spares the face, hands, and feet. Although dilated hair follicles filled with a hyperkeratotic plug in histology results have been reported, the lack of parakeratotic columns further excluded the disease.7 Treating PEODDN is challenging. Different therapeutic options, including topical steroids, retinoids, urea, salicylic acid, calcipotriol, systemic acitretin, phototherapy and cryotherapy, have demonstrated limited success.3,8For small and localized lesions, surgical excision can be considered. Carbon dioxide laser therapy, combined erbium/carbon dioxide laser, topical tazarotene, dithranol short-contact treatment, and photodynamic therapy seem to be effective for some patients.3Also, spontaneous partial regression, as in the current patient, has also been reported previously.8Regular follow-up is needed due to the possible progression to squamous cell carcinoma in some patients.9

scenario: A woman in her 50s presented with an edematous, massively enlarged right auricle. The patient had immigrated to Israel 9 years before admission. She was adamant that the lesion had been present since early childhood but had gradually increased with a recent appearance of foul-smelling otorrhea. On examination, the auricle was markedly enlarged, edematous, and encircled by an erythematous, indurated plaque partially covered with a fine scale (Figure 1A). Diascopy revealed an “apple jelly” appearance. There was no local or distant lymphadenopathy; general physical examination findings were unremarkable. Results of routine laboratory investigations, including complete blood cell count, biochemical profile, liver function tests, and chest radiography, were normal. An intradermal Mantoux test induced a 20-mm induration. Histopathologic evaluation of the cutaneous lesion revealed noncaseating granulomatous dermatitis involving the dermis (Figure 1B). High magnification demonstrated tuberculoid dermal granulomas composed of histiocytes and Langhans giant cells surrounded by lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate (Figure 1C). Results of polarized light examination and periodic acid–Schiff, Ziehl-Neelsen, Giemsa, Gram, and Grocott methenamine silver stains were negative for microorganisms.
explanation: A tissue culture was positive forMycobacterium tuberculosis. The clinicohistologic findings and isolation ofM tuberculosisconfirmed the diagnosis of lupus vulgaris (LV). A trial of quadruple antituberculous therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for the next 7 months resulted in a rapid clinical response. The patient was then lost to follow-up for several years, until 2020, when current physical examination revealed complete clinical resolution (Figure 2). Lupus vulgaris is the most common type of cutaneous tuberculosis. It is a paucibacillary disease characterized by a chronic and progressive course that develops in a previously sensitized host with strong delayed hypersensitivity to tuberculin. In Western countries, LV is more common in females and predominantly occurs in the head and neck region, while in tropical countries, it is more common in males and predominantly involves the lower limbs.1Lupus vulgaris may occur through hematogenous, lymphatic, or contiguous spread from a remote focus of disease elsewhere in the body. It may rarely follow primary inoculation or vaccination with bacille Calmette-Guérin.2Clinically, LV starts as an erythematous-brownish plaque that slowly expands over the years. A classic clinical sign is the apple jelly appearance on diascopy. Histologically, LV is characterized by a classic granulomatous tubercle with minimal caseation. The cellular inflammatory infiltrate includes epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, and mononuclear cells. Because bacilli are few and sparse in LV, acid-fast staining is rarely positive, and the yield of tissue cultures is also low.3-6In such cases, polymerase chain reaction for tissue mycobacterial DNA may increase diagnostic accuracy.6As patients with LV may have an active visceral focus of tuberculosis elsewhere, this should be sought out and excluded. To note, results of chest radiography are often normal, as the initial site of tuberculosis may be extrapulmonary. Originally, the termturkey earwas used to describe an enlarged, bluish-erythematous ear seen in lupus pernio.7However, this presentation is not specific and may be seen in other skin diseases. Williams et al3were, to our knowledge, the first to report LV with a turkey ear appearance and emphasized the need for a thorough clinical investigation in such cases. The chronic, relatively asymptomatic nature of LV may cause a significant delay in diagnosis. Indeed, the present patient’s case is similar to the few previously reported cases that were diagnosed as LV decades after presentation.3-5 The differential diagnosis of the present case includes inflammatory, infectious, and malignant conditions. Lupus pernio, a distinctive manifestation of cutaneous sarcoidosis, is characterized by violaceous papules and plaques, mostly affects adults, and is more common in Black women. The classic histopathological presentation of cutaneous sarcoidosis is the presence of “naked granulomas”—histiocytic granulomas devoid of prominent infiltrates of lymphocytes or plasma cells. Caseation is typically absent. Asteroid and Schaumann inclusion bodies may be seen within the multinucleated Langhans giant cells. Lupus pernio is often associated with systemic sarcoidal involvement. It is important to correctly differentiate between lupus pernio and LV because immunosuppressive treatment for the latter may have devastating consequences. Granulomatous mycosis fungoides is a rare subtype of mycosis fungoides characterized by infiltrates of atypical lymphocytes, histiocytes, and multinucleated giant cells.8The diagnosis may be supported by immunohistochemistry and T-cell receptor gene rearrangement. Interestingly, a case of granulomatous mycosis fungoides of the auricle resembling a turkey ear that was initially suspected as LV has been described in the literature.9 Leishmania recidivans develops in the site of previous infection that had healed and may mimic LV both clinically and histopathologically.10Definitive diagnosis requires the demonstration of Leishmania-Donovan bodies or positive result of polymerase chain reaction testing. Other conditions that could be considered in the differential diagnosis of this case are granulomatous fungal infections, tuberculoid leprosy, and granulomatous syphilis. Although cutaneous tuberculosis has become rare in past decades, massive immigration from endemic countries may contribute to its reemergence in other regions of the world. Therefore, dermatologists worldwide should still keep a high index of suspicion regarding atypical cases of cutaneous tuberculosis as presented here.

scenario: A 50-year-old woman with hypertension and epilepsy reported loud snoring associated with a 22.7-kg (50-lb) weight gain over the past 2 years. She described infrequent abrupt awakenings with a sensation of breathlessness but reported no witnessed apnea. She had fatigue but no headaches or excessive daytime sleepiness. Her blood pressure was 182/97 mm Hg, oxygen saturation was 98%, and body mass index was 51.3 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared). The remainder of her physical examination findings were normal. Laboratory evaluation revealed a serum bicarbonate level of 24 mEq/L (reference range, 23-29 mEq/L). The patient underwent home sleep testing using a home sleep test device. Results are presented in theTable.

options.A: Advise use of a wedge pillow to avoid sleeping in the supine position.
options.B: Initiate continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy.
options.D: Repeat the home sleep apnea test.

answer: Initiate continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy
distractors: Advise use of a wedge pillow to avoid sleeping in the supine position.
Repeat the home sleep apnea test.
explanation: B. Initiate continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects approximately 17% of women and 34% of men in the US, and it is diagnosed with a sleep study, performed either at home or in a laboratory.1The diagnosis of OSA is based on the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), consisting of the number of apnea and hypopnea events per hour of sleep. The presence of OSA is defined by an index level greater than 5 and is classified as mild (5-14.9 events/hour), moderate (15-29.9 events/hour), or severe (30 or more events/hour).1The risk of OSA can be assessed based on medical history and pretest prediction models, such as STOP-Bang.2 The 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline recommends that adults with signs and symptoms suggestive of moderate to severe OSA (eg, daytime sleepiness or unrefreshing sleep) undergo testing using home sleep apnea testing or polysomnography. For patients with significant cardiorespiratory disease, potential respiratory muscle weakness due to neuromuscular disease, awake hypoventilation, long-term opioid medication use, and history of stroke or severe insomnia, the guideline recommends use of polysomnography, rather than home sleep apnea testing.3 Compared with polysomnography, home sleep apnea testing devices monitor various physiological signals but do not provide a direct assessment of sleep because they do not incorporate electroencephalography, electro-oculography, and surface electromyography. Commonly used home sleep apnea testing devices (type 3) measure at least 4 physiological parameters, typically 2 respiratory variables (airflow and thoracic movement), a cardiac variable (electrocardiographic or heart rate), and pulse oximetry. Respiratory events are recorded if airflow amplitude and oxygen saturation both decrease during a segment of sleep. Other home sleep apnea testing devices (type 4) use peripheral arterial tonometry (PAT), a watch-sized computer worn on the wrist that measures the pulsatile arterial waveform associated with cardiac contractions. Respiratory events are recorded during episodes of oxyhemoglobin desaturation, heart rate acceleration, and dampening of arterial pulsation amplitude.4Home sleep apnea testing devices that use PAT often incorporate actigraphy, a device that measures limb movement and provides an indirect assessment of sleep.5 A meta-analysis of 19 studies6comparing type 3 home sleep apnea testing devices with polysomnography in adults with suspected sleep-disordered breathing reported that home sleep apnea testing had a sensitivity of 93% and a specificity of 60% if the AHI was 5 or more events per hour, and it reported a sensitivity of 79% and a specificity of 90% if the AHI was 30 or more events per hour. A meta-analysis of 20 studies7reported a diagnostic accuracy of 61% in classification of OSA severity category (normal, mild, moderate, and severe) comparing home sleep apnea testing vs polysomnography. A meta-analysis of PAT-based home sleep apnea testing8that included 13 trials reported a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 44% for patients with an AHI of 5 or more  events per hour, and it reported a sensitivity of 80% and a specificity of 90% for patients with an AHI of 30 or more events per hour. A comparison of concurrent polysomnography and PAT-based home sleep apnea testing device recordings of 500 patients suspected to have OSA found diagnostic concordance in 42% for mild, 41% for moderate, and 83% for severe OSA.9According to the 2022 Medicare fee schedule, reimbursement for home sleep apnea tests is $93.44 for type 3 devices and $164.03 for PAT-based devices.10 The patient’s AHI of 51.7 events per hour was consistent with severe OSA and was substantially worse while supine (94.2 events/hour) vs nonsupine (43.7 events/hour). The criterion standard for diagnosing OSA is an in-laboratory attended polysomnography that uses electroencephalography, electro-oculography, and surface electromyography to assess stages of sleep. Polysomnography also monitors airflow, electrocardiography, thoracic and abdominal respiratory effort, and pulse oximetry and provides continuous video monitoring and sound recording. Although polysomnography provides a comprehensive assessment of sleep, it is more expensive than a home sleep apnea testing device and requires travel to a sleep center, which is inconvenient for some patients. The patient received a CPAP machine with autotitrating CPAP pressure set at 6 to 16 cm H2O. Within several days of CPAP initiation, she noted a substantial decrease in daytime fatigue. Approximately 6 weeks later, data downloaded from her CPAP machine revealed CPAP use on 23 of 30 nights per month, at mean duration of 4.5 hours per night. While using the CPAP machine, the patient’s AHI decreased to 1.2 events per hour.

scenario: A 15-year-old adolescent girl who was taking an oral contraceptive presented to the emergency department with left lower quadrant abdominal pain that had developed gradually over a 3-day period. She had no associated nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, hematochezia, bloating, or anorexia. She reported no precipitating factors for the pain and had no history of pregnancy, abdominal surgery, or abdominal trauma. Over the previous 2 years, the patient had experienced similar intermittent episodes of abdominal pain lasting approximately 1 week. Results from laboratory tests, upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, and an abdominal computed tomography scan performed 1 year prior to presentation were normal. In the emergency department, her vital signs were normal and her body mass index was 20.4 (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters). Abdominal examination revealed no rigidity or guarding; however, a 1-cm point of maximal tenderness was identified in the left lower abdominal quadrant (Figure). During palpation of this 1-cm area, the pain increased when she lifted her head and tensed her abdominal muscles. She experienced cold hypoesthesia when an alcohol gauze pad was applied to this area and severe pain when the skin was pinched.

options.C: Inject a local anesthetic into the area of maximal tenderness

answer: Inject a local anesthetic into the area of maximal tenderness
explanation: Anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES) C. Inject a local anesthetic into the area of maximal tenderness The key to the correct diagnosis was recognition that the 1-cm point of maximal tenderness was localized to the outer rim of the rectus abdominis muscle.1Gabapentin (choice A) is not recommended because the diagnosis of postherpetic neuralgia is unlikely without a rash or dermatomal distribution of abdominal pain. Choice B is incorrect because the abdominal pain caused by celiac artery compression syndrome is typically epigastric and often increases after eating. Measuring urine porphobilinogen level (choice D) is unnecessary because acute intermittent porphyria typically causes diffuse abdominal pain. ACNES is an abdominal wall disorder that is 4 times more common in females than males. While the median age at diagnosis is 40 to 50 years, ACNES can affect individuals of any age, and the incidence increases during adolescence.1-3ACNES typically causes abdominal pain below the level of the umbilicus and is more frequently reported on the right side.2Up to 50% of patients with ACNES report visceral symptoms such as nausea, bloating, abdominal swelling, and loss of appetite.1 The pathophysiology of ACNES is thought to be related to compression and irritation of the intercostal nerve endings that pass through the rectus abdominus muscle and innervate the oblique muscles.1Abdominal muscle spasm results in progressive nerve entrapment, which perpetuates the pain.2Approximately one-third of individuals have an inciting event (abdominal surgery, abdominal trauma or sports-related injury, pregnancy, influenza infection) prior to onset of ACNES.1,2However, most patients do not report a clear precipitating event, and ACNES occurs spontaneously in 75% of adolescents who develop the condition.3 Although the exact incidence is unknown, ACNES is estimated to affect 1 in 2000 individuals in the general population.4In a study of unselected patients who presented to an emergency department with acute abdominal pain, 2% were diagnosed with ACNES.4The median interval between symptom onset and diagnosis of ACNES is 18 months.1In 1 study, the diagnosis was delayed for more than 5 years in 12% of patients.5Many of these patients had been diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome, fibromyalgia, complex regional pain syndrome, or rheumatoid arthritis.1 The diagnosis of ACNES is made based on history and characteristic clinical findings in patients who have abdominal pain in an area of 1 cm or less at the lateral border of the rectus abdominus muscle. Routine blood testing and imaging do not contribute to the diagnosis of ACNES but may exclude other causes of abdominal pain.2A positive Carnett test, defined as increased pain with head lifting and tensing of the abdominal muscles while the point of maximal tenderness is palpated, was reported in 87% of 1116 patients with ACNES1; 78% had severe pain with skin pinching, and 68% had altered skin perception to light touch or cold temperature in the affected area.1A diagnosis of ACNES is confirmed if an injection of 5 to 10 mL of local anesthetic (lidocaine) administered into the affected area with or without ultrasound guidance reduces pain by at least 50%.1,2,6 A single injection of lidocaine achieves immediate pain reduction in 86% of patients,5and approximately 10% to 20% of individuals with ACNES have persistent pain relief after a single injection.7Most patients with ACNES develop recurrent abdominal pain, which is typically treated with up to 2 additional injections of lidocaine.8In 1 study, pulsed radiofrequency therapy decreased abdominal pain in 50% of patients with ACNES, and 8% were pain-free at 15-month follow-up.9Neurectomy, consisting of surgical removal of intercostal nerve branches, may relieve pain for patients with recurrent or refractory pain despite multiple lidocaine injections.10 A subfascial injection of 5 mL of 1% lidocaine was administered under ultrasound guidance into the 1-cm area of maximal abdominal tenderness. One hour later, the patient reported a decrease in pain from 9 to 0 on a numeric pain rating scale that ranges from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst pain imaginable). At a clinic visit 9 months later, she reported no subsequent abdominal pain.

scenario: A 95-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 24 hours of abdominal pain, 2 weeks of diarrhea, and 3 months of intermittent abdominal bloating and anorexia. She was a farmer in rural Japan who did not drink alcohol and had been diagnosed with bullous pemphigoid 8 months prior, initially treated with prednisolone (15 mg daily). Her medications at presentation were prednisolone (8 mg daily) and lansoprazole. She had experienced 1 episode of dyspnea on exertion 2 weeks before presentation but reported no fevers, cough, wheeze, nausea or vomiting, hematochezia, or melena. In the emergency department, her temperature was 37.7 °C (99.9 °F); blood pressure, 110/56 mm Hg; heart rate, 125/min; and oxygen saturation, 95% on room air. On physical examination her lungs were clear to auscultation, and her abdomen was diffusely tender to palpation without rebound. Skin examination revealed purpuric macules and small thumbprint-like patches on the upper abdomen and central chest (Figure 1). Laboratory testing showed white blood cell count, 13 600/μL (89.9% neutrophils, 0.2% eosinophils); hemoglobin, 10.9 g/dL; serum sodium, 130 mEq/L (reference, 138-145 mEq/L); creatinine, 0.82 mg/dL (72.49 μmol/L); aspartate aminotransferase, 55 U/L (0.92 μkat/L) (reference, 13-30 U/L [0.22-0.50 μkat/L]); alanine aminotransferase, 54 U/L (0.90 μkat/L) (reference, 7-23 U/L [0.12-0.38 μkat/L]); and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, 31 mm/h (reference, 3-15 mm/h). Platelet count and prothrombin time were normal. Abdominal computed tomography with intravenous contrast revealed inflammation of the small intestine. The patient was treated with ampicillin/sulbactam, and her blood cultures grewKlebsiella pneumoniaeafter hospital admission.

explanation: A. Check stool for ova and parasites The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that chronic abdominal symptoms, abdominal purpuric macules and patches, and bacteremia in an immunosuppressed agricultural worker are characteristic findings of disseminated strongyloidiasis. A PCR panel for gastrointestinal pathogens (choice B) is useful to evaluate acute but not chronic diarrhea. Ordering measurement of ANCA level (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not have typical signs of ANCA-associated vasculitis. Choice D is incorrect because fungal infection does not typically cause purpura. Strongyloidiasis is caused byStrongyloides stercoralis, an intestinal helminth, and affects approximately 370 million people worldwide, with a prevalence of 10% to 40% in people living in tropical and subtropical regions.1In the US, strongyloidiasis is most commonly diagnosed in people who have immigrated or in travelers returning from high-prevalence regions; however,S stercoralisis endemic in the southeastern US.2,3 Infection withS stercoralistypically occurs when filariform larvae in soil penetrate the skin of individuals who walk barefoot on contaminated soil. The larvae migrate through the venous circulation to the lungs and ascend the trachea to the oropharynx, where they are swallowed.1After ingestion, the larvae lodge in the small intestine and produce eggs that become rhabditiform larvae that are excreted in stool.3,4Some larvae mature into filariform larvae, which penetrate the colonic wall or perianal skin, leading to reinfection of the host (autoinfection).1This process results in persistentS stercoralisinfection. Chronic strongyloidiasis develops when acute strongyloidiasis is not treated and is perpetuated by autoinfection via the gastrointestinal tract, peritoneum, and lungs, which are directly involved in the life cycle ofS stercoralis.1Immunocompetent patients with chronic strongyloidiasis are often asymptomatic or have only mild abdominal symptoms, minor skin manifestations, and eosinophilia ranging from 5% to 15%.1 Hyperinfection syndrome, defined by an accelerated rate of autoinfection, typically occurs when patients with chronic strongyloidiasis develop impaired cell-mediated immunity due to corticosteroids, human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1), chemotherapy, solid organ transplant, or malnutrition.3Disseminated strongyloidiasis can develop after hyperinfection and involves propagation ofS stercoralisto organs outside the typical autoinfection cycle, such as the skin, brain, heart, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, kidneys, ovaries, and skeletal muscle.1,5 Patients with hyperinfection syndrome and disseminated strongyloidiasis may experience small bowel obstruction due to the large quantity of intestinal larvae, and gastrointestinal bleeding from intestinal invasion, in addition to abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, and vomiting.6Pulmonary symptoms may include cough, shortness of breath, wheeze, and hemorrhagic pneumonitis.3Periumbilical purpura in the pattern of a thumbprint results from larval invasion into the umbilical vein; this is rare but pathognomonic for disseminated strongyloidiasis.6,7Eosinophilia is often absent in hyperinfection syndrome and disseminated strongyloidiasis.3,4 Patients with hyperinfection syndrome and disseminated strongyloidiasis have abundant larvae, which can be easily detected on examination of stool, sputum, and pleural or cerebrospinal fluid.5Although no evidence-based guidelines exist for treatment of severe strongyloidiasis, daily ivermectin (200 μg/kg) is typically prescribed for a minimum of 2 weeks and until stool examination is negative for 2 weeks.6,8Despite treatment, mortality associated with hyperinfection syndrome and disseminated strongyloidiasis has been reported as 69% to 85%,1,5due to complications such as peritonitis, respiratory failure, meningitis, and bacteremia caused by enteric bacterial translocation that accompanies larval invasion of the intestines.3,5,6,9 Strongyloides stercoralislarvae were detected in the patient’s stool and induced sputum (Figure 2). She was treated with ivermectin (9 mg orally daily for 14 days). Antibody testing for HTLV-1 was negative. The patient’s mental status declined, and a lumbar puncture was performed on hospital day 10.Enterococcus faeciumwas identified in cerebrospinal fluid culture, and her antibiotics were changed to vancomycin and meropenem. Four weeks after hospital admission, the patient died of upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

scenario: An 18-year-old woman with no significant medical history and no history of sexual intercourse presented for evaluation of pharyngitis and tonsillar exudates of 1 week duration. She reported neck swelling and an occasional dry cough but no fevers, chills, trismus, headache, dyspnea, chest pain, abdominal pain, fatigue, or rash. One week prior to presentation, she visited an urgent care clinic for evaluation of pharyngitis and white exudates on her tonsils. Results of a rapid strep test and heterophile antibody test (monospot) were negative. A throat culture was obtained and she was prescribed amoxicillin (500 mg twice daily for 10 days) for possible group A streptococcal infection. Despite taking antibiotics for 7 days, she had no improvement in her symptoms. One day prior to presentation, the urgent care clinic notified the patient that her throat culture results were negative. On presentation, the patient was in no acute distress and had normal vital signs. She had bilateral white tonsillar exudates and posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, but no exudate was observed elsewhere in the oral cavity and the uvula was midline (Figure). There was no axillary or inguinal adenopathy and no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. The remainder of the physical examination was normal.

options.C: Recheck a rapid heterophile antibody test
options.D: Treat with an oral antifungal medication

answer: Recheck a rapid heterophile antibody test
distractors: Obtain an ultrasound of the neck
Treat with an oral antifungal medication
explanation: C. Recheck a rapid heterophile antibody test The key to the correct diagnosis is recognition that infectious mononucleosis can present without constitutional symptoms of fever and fatigue and that a rapid heterophile antibody test result may be falsely negative early in the illness. Obtaining an ultrasound of the neck (choice A) is incorrect because peritonsillar abscess is unlikely without fever, trismus, and uvula deviation. Prescribing azithromycin (choice B) is inappropriate. Moreover, an antibiotic should not have been prescribed initially by the urgent care center because this patient had a negative rapid strep test result and had only 2 of 4 Centor criteria1for streptococcal pharyngitis. The tonsillar exudates were present before starting antibiotics and no abnormalities were noted on the tongue, so thrush is unlikely and therefore treatment with an antifungal medication (choice D) is not recommended. Infectious mononucleosis is a syndrome caused by a viral infection that typically presents with the triad of fever, lymphadenopathy, and pharyngitis. Fatigue, splenomegaly, and atypical lymphocytosis of greater than or equal to 10% are also common features of infectious mononucleosis.2However, some patients have relatively mild disease, presenting only with oropharyngotonsillitis. Others may have fever and lymphadenopathy without pharyngitis. Infectious mononucleosis in adults older than 40 years is less likely to present with lymphadenopathy and pharyngitis and more likely to be associated with prolonged fevers, hepatitis, cholestasis, and hepatomegaly.3 Approximately 90% of infectious mononucleosis diagnoses are caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a member of the herpesvirus family. The remainder are caused by cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, and acute HIV. EBV infection is common, with more than 95% of all adults worldwide estimated to be seropositive for EBV.4EBV is typically transmitted person-to-person via exposure to infected saliva through kissing, sharing of food or drink, coughing, and, less commonly, through sexual transmission. Rarely, EBV can be transmitted by blood transfusion, solid organ transplant, or hematopoietic stem cell transplant.5The incubation period between viral infection and symptom onset is typically 4 to 8 weeks. Infectious mononucleosis presents most commonly in teenagers and young adults in high-income countries. In developing countries, EBV infection tends to occur in early childhood and is often asymptomatic or presents as a nonspecific illness.6Older adults are less likely to develop infectious mononucleosis because of immunity acquired from EBV infection earlier in life. The differential diagnosis for the infectious mononucleosis triad of fever, lymphadenopathy, and pharyngitis includes infection with group A streptococcus, toxoplasma gondii, lymphoma, or drug reaction to certain anticonvulsant medications or antibiotics. Diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis is typically performed by demonstration of heterophile antibodies, which develop in response to infection with EBV and can be detected with rapid diagnostic tests using a latex agglutination assay or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay technique. The sensitivity of rapid tests for heterophile antibodies is estimated at 70% to 92% and specificity as 96% to 100%,7but false-negatives occur in approximately 25% of patients with infectious mononucleosis within the first week of infection.8If the result of a rapid test for heterophile antibodies is negative early in the course of illness and suspicion for infectious mononucleosis remains high, the rapid test should be repeated, EBV-specific antibodies can be obtained, or both. No antiviral medications are effective against infectious mononucleosis. Most patients with infectious mononucleosis recover from pharyngitis within 1 to 2 weeks. Fatigue typically lasts several weeks beyond the resolution of pharyngitis and may persist for months.9There is a small but potentially fatal risk of splenic rupture, estimated at 0.1%, up to 8 weeks after onset of infectious mononucleosis.10 The patient underwent a repeat rapid heterophile antibody test, which resulted in a positive monospot test result. The patient took ibuprofen and acetaminophen for the next week. Fourteen days later, all symptoms had completely resolved.

scenario: A 25-year-old woman with migraines for 10 years presented with palpitations, fatigue, and worsening migraines. Her heart rate was 93 beats/min and blood pressure was 120/92 mm Hg. Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram results were normal. Subsequent 48-hour Holter monitoring showed sinus tachycardia with a mean heart rate of 108 beats/min. Metoprolol succinate (25 mg daily) was started. Six months later, she was admitted to the hospital with 1 day of fevers, nausea, and right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Her temperature was 38.7 °C (101.7 °F); heart rate, 103 beats/min; and blood pressure, 138/89 mm Hg. Abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) showed a left anterior pararenal retroperitoneal mass. Abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with and without intravenous contrast showed a 4.0 × 3.5–cm T1 and T2 hypointense, enhancing infrarenal left para-aortic mass without local tissue or vascular invasion (Figure). Plasma normetanephrine concentration was 907 pg/mL (reference, 0-145 pg/mL) and plasma metanephrine concentration was within reference range.

options.D: Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control)

answer: Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control)
explanation: D. Start doxazosin (2 mg twice daily, titrating up as needed to maintain blood pressure control) The key to the correct diagnosis is presence of an elevated normetanephrine concentration in a patient with a retroperitoneal mass. Choice A is not recommended because biopsy can precipitate catecholamine crisis, consisting of a surge of catecholamine release that may cause hypertensive emergency, myocardial infarction, stroke, or aortic dissection. Discontinuing metoprolol succinate (choice B) is incorrect because β-blockers can prevent reflex tachycardia associated with α-1 adrenergic blocker medications, recommended for preoperative management of paragangliomas. Gallium-68 DOTATATE imaging (choice C) is not indicated because additional imaging is not necessary for diagnosis. Tumors of the autonomic nervous system that arise from chromaffin tissue (neural tissue that produces and secretes catecholamines) include pheochromocytomas (located in the adrenal medulla) and paragangliomas (located in sympathetic extra-adrenal ganglia). Paragangliomas are rare (estimated incidence of up to 0.95 cases per 100 000 people annually), and incidence does not differ by sex.1,2Sympathetic paragangliomas usually secrete catecholamines and metanephrines. Parasympathetic paragangliomas, which are typically located in the head and neck region, are usually nonsecretory.3,4 Paragangliomas may be identified as an incidental finding on an imaging study of the abdomen, pelvis, head, neck, or thorax. However, most patients typically experience palpitations, hypertension, anxiety, and/or syncope (due to secretion of epinephrine) or headaches, sweating, and/or persistent hypertension (due to secretion of norepinephrine).5Due to mass effect, head and neck paragangliomas can cause symptoms such as hoarseness and dysphagia, and retroperitoneal paragangliomas may cause local compression symptoms. Both plasma and urine metanephrine tests have more than a 90% sensitivity for diagnosis of paragangliomas. However, plasma metanephrine testing is favored due to ease of collection and higher specificity (79%-98%) compared with 24-hour urine testing (69%-95%).3Metanephrine or normetanephrine concentrations at least 4 times above the upper limit of normal are consistent with diagnosis of paraganglioma. Patients diagnosed with a paraganglioma based on biochemical testing should undergo abdominal CT or MRI imaging, with and without contrast. Nearly all (99%) of paragangliomas have Hounsfield unit density greater than  10 on unenhanced CT scan.6,7Functional imaging using nuclear scans such as gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/CT can be helpful to assess for metastases. Ga-DOTATATE is a radiotracer that binds to somatostatin receptors, which are found on paragangliomas. Guidelines recommend germline genetic testing for all patients diagnosed with paraganglioma.8,9Germline gene variants are found in up to 40% of patients with paragangliomas, who have a high prevalence of hereditary syndromes such as von Hippel–Lindau, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, neurofibromatosis type 1, and succinate dehydrogenase gene (SDHx) variant–related tumors.8Identifying a genetic germline variant can help guide management, including surveillance for associated tumors (such as kidney cancer and gastrointestinal stromal tumor in patients withSDHxgene variants) and screening of first-degree family members. First-line treatment of paraganglioma is surgical resection. Prior to surgery, most patients with paraganglioma, and especially those with elevated catecholamine levels, should be treated with an α-adrenergic blocker medication with the nonselective α-1/2–adrenoceptor blocker (phenoxybenzamine) or a selective competitive α-1–adrenoceptor blocker (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin). These medications prevent excessive vasoconstriction and severe hypertension caused by catecholamine release from the tumor.10β-Adrenergic blockers may be added to treat tachycardia but only after adequate α blockade has been achieved, because unopposed α receptor stimulation may precipitate hypertensive crisis. To assess for recurrence, all patients with paraganglioma should undergo plasma metanephrine and catecholamine testing within 2 months of surgical resection, with repeat testing every 6 to 12 months depending on the risk of recurrence. Patients withSDHBgermline gene variants are recommended to undergo annual biochemical screening with plasma metanephrines and catecholamines and biennial whole-body MRI imaging. The patient was treated with doxazosin (4 mg twice daily), and metoprolol succinate was increased to 50 mg twice daily. Three weeks after presentation, open resection of the paraganglioma was performed, and histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of paraganglioma. After surgery, her palpitations and fatigue resolved, and her migraines slowly improved, resolving after about 1 year. She underwent testing using a panel of 12 genes associated with hereditary paraganglioma, which revealed a pathogenic variant in theSDHBgene. Annual plasma metanephrine concentrations have been normal, and MRI imaging of the neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis has not identified any lesions, with the most recent scan performed 6 years after presentation.

scenario: A 36-year-old man presented for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes 2 months after undergoing a liver transplant for acute-on-chronic liver failure due to alcohol-associated hepatitis. He had metabolic comorbidities including obesity (body mass index of 30.6) and dyslipidemia. After the liver transplant, there was no evidence of organ rejection or biliary complications. He was asymptomatic and reported last alcohol use was prior to liver transplant. Vital signs were normal and physical examination revealed a well-healed abdominal surgical scar. Serum alcohol level was undetectable and urine drug screening results were positive for cannabinoids. Liver ultrasonography findings were normal. Liver biopsy showed 50% to 60% macrovesicular steatosis (normal <5%), mild portal inflammation, scattered apoptotic bodies, and hepatocyte ballooning (Table 1).

options.A: Acute rejection of the transplanted liver.

distractors: Acute rejection of the transplanted liver.
explanation: Phosphatidylethanol (PEth) is a whole blood marker of alcohol that can be detectable for up to 4 weeks after alcohol consumption. PEth is not a single molecule. It is a group of phospholipid homologues with a phosphoethanol head and 2 carboxylic acid side chains that attach to the erythrocyte surface in the presence of blood ethanol, catalyzed by the enzyme phospholipase D.1PEth species are categorized by the number of carbon atoms (typically 14-22) and double bonds; the 16:0/18:1 and 16:0/18:2 homologues are the most common forms.1Testing for PEth can be performed using dried blood spots or whole blood collected in ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid tubes. PEth is a direct biomarker of alcohol that forms after ethanol consumption. A study of 16 recently abstinent volunteers who consumed alcohol to achieve a blood alcohol concentration of 1 g/kg (single ingestion of 110-230 mL of 40% vodka) demonstrated that PEth was detectable within 1 hour of alcohol consumption, peaked at 8 hours, and was detectable for 3 to 12 days after consumption, with a mean half-life of 3 days.2A PEth concentration less than 20 ng/mL indicates minimal or no recent alcohol consumption and a PEth concentration greater than 200 ng/mL correlates with heavy alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily). A standard drink is defined as equivalent to 12 fl oz of beer, 5 fl oz of wine, or 1.5 fl oz of distilled spirits.3 PEth formation and degradation are not affected by age, sex, or organ dysfunction such as chronic kidney disease or hepatic dysfunction.1The rate of PEth formation depends on the level and activity of phospholipase D, which varies among individuals. The degradation rate of PEth also varies, with an estimated mean half-life of 4 to 10 days. PEth may be detectable up to 5 weeks after heavy alcohol consumption.1Blood PEth level increases with higher quantity and frequency of alcohol consumption and decreases with time elapsed since last ingestion of alcohol. A false-positive PEth test result may occur if an individual receives a blood transfusion from a person who recently consumed alcohol, due to PEth on donated erythrocytes.4Falsely low PEth concentrations may occur in patients with low haptoglobin levels, consistent with intravascular hemolysis.5PEth has a sensitivity of 94.5% to 99% and a specificity of 100% for high levels of alcohol consumption (≥4 standard drinks daily) and a sensitivity of 81.8% for lower levels of alcohol ingestion.6In 2024, Medicare reimbursement was $114.43 for PEth testing.7 The patient’s PEth concentration of 137 ng/dL was consistent with recent alcohol ingestion despite his undetectable serum alcohol level and initial report of no recent alcohol consumption. Blood, breath, and urine alcohol levels detect alcohol consumed in the preceding 12 to 24 hours. Ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate are formed by enzymatic conjugation of ethanol with glucuronic acid and sulfate, respectively, and may be detected in urine within 2 to 3 hours of alcohol consumption and remain detectable for 4 to 5 days after consumption.8False-positive urinary ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate test results may occur due to kidney dysfunction or bacterial fermentation in the urine (eg, cystitis); false-negative results may occur with use of diuretics or intentional dilution of urine specimens.1Ethyl glucuronide can be detected in hair and nails for approximately 2 months after alcohol cessation in frequent drinkers9(Table 2).7,10Direct alcohol biomarkers (PEth and ethyl glucuronide) have been studied and validated in patients with and without liver disease. Additional testing revealed a urine ethyl sulfate level of 45 475 ng/mL (reference, <100 ng/mL) and urine ethyl glucuronide level of >10 000 ng/mL (reference, <500 ng/mL). The patient disclosed consuming 5 shots of vodka daily for 7 days prior to presentation. He was prescribed naltrexone and referred to an intensive outpatient program for alcohol use disorder. Liver chemistries were normal 2 weeks after presentation and PEth was undetectable 3 weeks later. In the clinic 2 months later, he reported alcohol abstinence; was meeting with his psychotherapy, psychiatry, and social work teams; and had undetectable blood PEth levels and normal liver graft function.

scenario: A 63-year-old woman with osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea treated with nasal continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) presented with several months of worsening pain in her hands (first metacarpophalangeal joints), wrists, and feet. Radiographs of the hands and wrists performed 1 month prior showed degenerative changes but no bone erosions. Her vital signs and physical examination findings were normal. She had no redness, warmth, or swelling of any joints, and her skin examination was unremarkable. However, a deformity of the nasal bridge was noted after she was asked to remove her face mask, which she was wearing as required during the COVID-19 pandemic (Figure). She reported no history of facial trauma, recent travel, illicit drug use, or high-risk sexual behavior. The nasal deformity, which she attributed to use of her CPAP mask, had developed gradually over the past several years. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count (WBC) of 7700/uL, hemoglobin level of 13.2 mg/dL, and platelet count of 404 × 103/μL. Creatinine was 1.2 mg/dL (baseline, 0.83 mg/dL); erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 43 mm/h (reference range, 0-40 mm/h) and C-reactive protein was 23 mg/L (reference range, 0-10 mg/L). Her urinalysis had more than 30 white blood cells/high-power field (HPF), more than 30 red blood cells/HPF, and 2+ protein. Urine sediment microscopy showed red blood cell casts. The patient was referred for a kidney biopsy.

Obtain conventional angiography of the aorta and renal arteries
Order rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test
explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) with rapidly progressive pauci-immune glomerulonephritis (RPGN) A. Check antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) titers The key to the correct diagnosis was the presence of subacute joint pain along with a saddle nose deformity, which was revealed when the patient removed her face mask. The differential diagnosis of saddle nose deformity includes relapsing polychondritis, sarcoidosis, granulomatous infections (such as syphilis and leprosy), neoplasms, intranasal drug use, and trauma. However, the combination of saddle nose deformity, arthralgias, and acute kidney injury with red blood cell casts and proteinuria is highly suggestive of systemic small-vessel vasculitis such as GPA. Although lupus nephritis and scleroderma renal crisis may cause hematuria, proteinuria, and worsening kidney function, these diseases are not associated with saddle nose deformity, so checking antinuclear antibodies and complement levels (choice B) is less useful. Conventional angiography of the aorta and renal arteries (choice C) can identify renal artery aneurysms and stenoses. However, a medium-vessel vasculitis affecting the renal arteries, such as polyarteritis nodosa, does not typically present with glomerulonephritis. While checking RPR and a fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test (choice D) is reasonable to work up causes of saddle nose deformity, syphilis does not typically cause glomerulonephritis. GPA, formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis, is a potentially life-threatening small-vessel vasculitis characterized by the presence of ANCA targeting neutrophil-specific granule proteins. GPA causes necrotizing granulomatous inflammation in small blood vessels throughout the body, most commonly affecting the capillary beds of the kidneys, lungs, and skin. GPA affects men and women equally and is rare, with an incidence of 0.4 to 11.9 cases per million person-years and prevalence of 2.3 to 146.0 cases per million persons.1 GPA may cause inflammation of the upper respiratory tract, resulting in crusting rhinitis, otitis, subglottic stenosis, and sinusitis. Chronic granulomatous sinusitis due to GPA can lead to bone and cartilage destruction, resulting in collapse of the nasal bridge, which causes the appearance of a saddle nose deformity. GPA also commonly affects the lower respiratory tract (lung granuloma, alveolar hemorrhage), kidney (pauci-immune glomerulonephritis), and skin (palpable purpura). Systemic symptoms such as arthralgias, fever, and fatigue are frequently experienced by patients with GPA. Kidney involvement, often in the form of RPGN, occurs in up to 70% of patients with GPA. Early diagnosis of GPA is important to avoid progression to kidney failure, which occurs in approximately one quarter of patients with RPGN.2 Patients with GPA most commonly have a cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) pattern and antibodies directed against proteinase 3 (PR3), which is located in neutrophils and monocytes. However, a smaller proportion of patients demonstrate a perinuclear staining pattern (p-ANCA) with antibodies typically directed against myeloperoxidase (MPO).1Although kidney biopsy is not required to diagnose GPA, it is helpful to confirm the diagnosis of GPA in the setting of pulmonary-renal syndrome (to exclude anti–glomerular basement membrane disease) or in patients with suspected GPA but negative ANCA and absence of antibodies directed against MPO or PR3. Induction therapy for patients with organ-threatening complications of GPA includes rituximab and high-dose glucocorticoids.3Cyclophosphamide can also be used for induction of remission,4but it may be associated with greater toxicity than rituximab.5-7For maintenance of remission, the most commonly used medications are rituximab, methotrexate, or azathioprine.8 Blood testing in this patient revealed p-ANCA at 1:160 dilution and presence of anti-MPO antibodies. Kidney biopsy demonstrated a pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis, confirming the diagnosis of GPA. She was initially treated with rituximab and prednisone, 1 mg/kg/d. Prednisone was tapered over the next 6 months to her current dose of 5 mg/d, with resolution of her joint pain. At 15 months from induction of remission, she continues to receive rituximab as maintenance therapy and her kidney function has recovered to baseline. Her nasal deformity was successfully treated with reconstructive surgery.

scenario: A 69-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of progressive skin discoloration. His medical history included chronic kidney disease, chronic hepatitis C infection, cirrhosis, ischemic cardiomyopathy with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), and atrial fibrillation with prophylactic apixaban. He had recurrent staphylococcus bacteremia due to infection of an ICD lead and had been treated for the past 6 months with minocycline, 100 mg twice daily. His arms had been purple and bruise-like for several years but turned a near black color 1 month ago. He reported no discoloration of his sweat or urine. He had no history of malnutrition and reported infrequent alcohol use. Physical examination showed dense blue-black skin pigmentation of his forearms, dorsal hands, legs, and dorsal feet, as well as blue discoloration of his sclerae and teeth (Figure 1). He had normal-colored nails and oral mucosa. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count of 15 800/μL (reference range, 4000-11 000/μL), hemoglobin of 10.7 g/dL (reference, 13.5-17.5 g/dL), platelet count of 58 000/μL (reference, 150 000-400 000/μL), and INR of 1.8 (reference, 0.8-1.1). Complete metabolic panel showed increased creatinine (1.51 mg/dL; reference, 0.64-1.27 mg/dL) and elevated total bilirubin (1.7 mg/dL; reference range, 0.3-1.2 mg/dL). His estimated glomerular filtration rate was 40 mL/min/1.73 m2.
explanation: The keys to the correct diagnosis are the blue-black color of the pigmentation, the location on the distal extremities, and the involvement of sclerae and teeth. Potential etiologies for blue skin discoloration include drug-induced (eg, amiodarone, minocycline, hydroxychloroquine, and fluoroquinolones1), exposure to silver (argyria) or gold salts (chrysiasis), and deposition of pigmented fibers due to an inherited enzyme deficiency (endogenous ochronosis or alkaptonuria) or hydroquinone use (exogenous ochronosis).2Given this patient’s ongoing minocycline use, discontinuing minocycline is the best answer. This patient’s ecchymoses, most prominent at his proximal forearms, represent a distinct process from the blue-black pigmentation caused by minocycline. The ecchymoses were due to his use of apixaban, thrombocytopenia, bleeding diathesis, and skin fragility from age and sun exposure and would not necessitate stopping apixaban (choice A). Hemochromatosis (choice C) causes skin dyspigmentation that is typically diffuse and brown or slate-gray.3Pellagra, caused by deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) (choice D), presents with a photodistributed rash; however, the rash is red or brown and does not discolor sclerae or teeth.2 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation presents as blue-hued pigmentation of the skin that may also involve the sclerae, nails, teeth, and oral mucosa. The reported incidence varies from 2% to 15% in patients treated for acne to 41% to 54% in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and orthopedic infections, respectively.4-6 Although minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation is a clinical diagnosis, skin biopsy can confirm the diagnosis and reveals subepidermal deposition of granular black pigment both interstitially and intracellularly (Figure 2). The pigment reacts positively with staining techniques used to detect iron and/or melanin (Perl’s Prussian blue and Fontana-Masson, respectively). In contrast, ecchymoses stain positive for iron only. While the mechanism of hyperpigmentation remains unclear, histopathologic studies indicate that minocycline and/or its metabolites likely form insoluble complexes with iron that deposit in tissue.7 Minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation is classified into 3 types based on clinical findings and histologic staining, though these categories may overlap. In type I, blue pigmentation is found in scars, commonly facial acne scars, and stains positive for iron only. In type II, blue pigmentation affects normal skin, typically on the extremities, and stains positive for both iron and melanin. Type III presents with muddy brown discoloration most prominent in sun-exposed skin and stains positive for melanin.8 This patient’s presentation was consistent with type II hyperpigmentation and notable for both the striking degree of pigmentation and for its rapid development after only 6 months of treatment. Most minocycline-induced hyperpigmentation occurs after a year, though small case series have reported pigmentation after only a few weeks.5,6,9Several characteristics of this patient may have contributed to the more rapid onset, including the longstanding purpura on his arms, which increases dermal iron available for chelation, as well as hepatic and kidney disease, which impair drug metabolism and excretion. Minocycline-induced cutaneous hyperpigmentation persists after drug cessation and is challenging to treat. Given the small size of the pigment particle, treatment is best approached with picosecond or Q-switched lasers.10In addition to its effects on skin pigmentation, minocycline use in children can result in permanent teeth discoloration and bone hypoplasia and should be avoided during pregnancy and in children younger than 8 years old.2 Minocycline was discontinued and daptomycin was started in its place. The patient declined treatment for the pigmentation changes because they were not bothersome to him.

scenario: A 24-year-old man presented with progressive gait instability. Although this started in childhood as a tendency to drag his left leg and trip, he could keep his balance on a skateboard until the age of 14 years. He had no significant medical history. There was neither family history of neurological illnesses nor consanguinity. Upon neurologic examination, he had normal cognition, slight dysarthria, impaired smooth pursuit, subtle tremor of both hands, left-sided spasticity, normal muscle strength, mildly impaired joint position sense in his toes bilaterally, and hyperreflexia with increased patellar and ankle jerk reflexes. Pes cavus and Babinski sign were present bilaterally as well as truncal and appendicular ataxia. Several teeth were absent (hypodontia) or too small (microdontia). Electrocardiogram results were normal. Complete blood cell count, thyroid, liver, and kidney function were within normal limits. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain and upper spinal cord (Figure 1) showed marked spinal cord atrophy with an anterior-posterior width of 4 mm, isolated hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles, and atrophy of the isthmus of the corpus callosum.

options.C: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay

distractors: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
explanation: The clinical and radiological findings were consistent with POLR3A-related spastic ataxia and exome sequencing revealed a compound heterozygousPOLR3Amutation (c.2000T>A [p.Leu667*]/c.1909 + 22G>A). The first variant (p.Leu667*) has not been previously reported but causes a loss of function and is therefore considered likely pathogenic. The second (intronic) mutation (c.1909 + 22G>A) causes a cryptic splice site, leading to the production of both wild-type and aberrant transcripts. It is considered pathogenic based on cosegregation data and predicts a more benign phenotype.1 POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is an autosomal recessively inherited disease. While diffuse hypomyelination/leukodystrophy has originally been described as the classic radiological finding, this does not seem to be obligate for all POLR3A-related disorders.2The cardinal features of the spastic ataxia subtype are typically adolescent-onset progressive gait abnormality and teeth deformities.1Panoramic dental radiography (Figure 2) for this patient corroborated the absence of several teeth, microdontia, interdental spacing, and a rectangular shape of several teeth known as “taurodontia,” caused by enlarged pulp chambers. Common radiographic features include spinal cord atrophy, mild atrophy of cerebellum and corpus callosum, and hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles.3,4Compound heterozygous POLR3A mutations have been identified in 3% of patients who present with otherwise genetically unexplained spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.1,5 POLR3A mutations have been linked to other genetic syndromes, including 4H leukodystrophy (consisting of hypomyelination, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hypodontia) and Wiedemann-Rautenstrauch syndrome, a recognizable neonatal syndrome causing premature aging.3The phenotypic differences between these disorders are thought to arise from the different functional effects of underlying POLR3A mutations.3 Hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7 (SPG7) is an alternative diagnosis that should be considered. SPG7 presents as spastic ataxia or isolated cerebellar ataxia. Likely pathogenic mutations in the SPG7 gene are found in 18.6% of patients with unexplained ataxia, making it one of the most common genetic causes. MRI for patients with SPG7 demonstrates cerebellar atrophy and sometimes atrophy of the medial and lateral rectus muscle.6Although ataxia and pyramidal signs are the most common clinical features, a more complex phenotype does occur with neuro-ophthalmological findings like nystagmus, partial ophthalmoparesis, slow saccades, or optic neuropathy.6This was not seen in this patient. To the best of our knowledge, hypodontia has not been described in SPG7, making it a less probable diagnosis. Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay is an uncommon heredodegenerative disease characterized by early-onset ataxia associated with spasticity. Brain MRI shows cerebellar vermis atrophy and linear T2-hypointensities in the pons.7The disease is associated with variable degrees of peripheral neuropathy, pes cavus, and retinal fiber hypertrophy that is almost pathognomonic and was not seen in this patient. Friedreich ataxia (FRDA) is the most common and thus the most important alternative diagnosis. FRDA has a typical onset before age 25 years. It manifests as a spastic ataxia with pes cavus, cardiac problems, and variable loss of reflexes.8MRI of the spinal cord looks similar to POLR3A.7,9Therefore, distinguishing between POLR3A and FRDA often relies heavily on accompanying clinical signs and genetic testing. In a large cohort of 650 patients with genetically confirmed FRDA, the most frequent clinical features beyond ataxia were abnormal eye movements (90.5%), scoliosis (73.5%), deformities of the feet (58.8%), urinary dysfunction (42.8%), and cardiomyopathy and cardiac hypertrophy (40.3%), followed by decreased visual acuity (36.8%).10These were not present in this patient. Additionally, genetic testing for FRDA was negative, with less than 27 GAA repeats on both alleles of the FXN gene. In summary, POLR3A-related spastic ataxia is a not-so-rare autosomal recessively inherited disease with spastic/ataxic gait and hypodontia as the main clinical features. Cases carrying c.1909 + 22G>A demonstrate spinal cord atrophy and hyperintensities along the superior cerebellar peduncles instead of diffuse leukodystrophy.

scenario: A 31-year-old man with insidious onset of limited mobility of joints visited our clinic for evaluation. Six months prior, he found his palms could not make full contact with each other (the “prayer sign”). He had not been able to fully clench his fists for 2 months or squat for the past 10 days. No erythema, edema, or sclerotic skin plaque had been found on his limbs or trunk. No Raynaud phenomenon had occurred. His medical and family histories were unremarkable. On examination, he showed bilateral limited mobility of interphalangeal (hands), metacarpophalangeal, wrist, interphalangeal (feet), metatarsophalangeal, and ankle joints (Video). No muscular atrophy or sclerodactyly was found. The prayer sign (Figure 1A) and the “groove sign” (Figure 1B) were observed. Blood test results indicated eosinophilia (absolute eosinophil count, 1300 μL; reference, <500μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR, 31 mm/h; reference, <15 mm/h) and C-reactive protein (CRP, 3.01 mg/dL; reference, <0.8 mg/dL [to convert to mg/L, multiply by 10]). Liver and kidney function tests, creatine kinase level, electrolyte level, thyroid function, globulin concentration, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) level were unremarkable. Electrocardiogram, cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging, and plain radiographs of hands, wrists, feet, and ankles were normal. Nerve conduction studies performed in all 4 limbs were normal. Electromyography (EMG) showed spontaneous activities in muscles of limbs, including fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves (1+ or 2+). Myotonic discharges were seen in bilateral extensor digitorum.
explanation: Insidious onset of bilaterally limited joint mobility is infrequently seen by neurologists. EMG showed electrical myotonia, reminiscent of myotonic dystrophy (choice A).1However, myotonic dystrophy is characterized by abnormally slow or delayed muscle relaxation following a normal muscle contraction,1which was absent in this patient. Limited joint mobility and the prayer sign can be seen in systemic sclerosis (choice B).2However, the negative ANA test results and the absence of Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and internal organ involvement helped exclude systemic sclerosis.3Limited mobility of joints, peripheral eosinophilia, and increased ESR and CRP can be found in deep morphea (choice C), a rare subtype of morphea that primarily involves the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue and may extend to underlying fascia and muscle.4Nevertheless, the symmetrical distribution of joint involvement, histology displaying preferential fascial inflammation (Figure 2), and the absence of sclerotic skin plaque in this patient point to the diagnosis of eosinophilic fasciitis (EF) over deep morphea. EF is a rare disorder characterized by the induration of fascia and skin, preceded by the abrupt onset of erythema and nonpitting edema, resulting in limited mobility of the underlying joints.3The disease can have an insidious onset.5The appearance of orange peel caused by skin induration and the groove sign, which is probably due to the relative sparing of the epidermis and superficial dermis by the fibrotic process, are typical signs of established EF.3Occasionally, EF can present without skin involvement.6,7Sclerodactyly and Raynaud phenomenon are usually absent. Laboratory findings of EF include peripheral eosinophilia, increased ESR and CRP level, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, and negative ANA test results.3The results of biopsy containing skin, fascia, and muscle conducted at the left gastrocnemius of this patient showed inflammatory cell infiltrate mainly in the fascia (composed primarily of lymphocytes and eosinophils) (Figure 2) and some subjacent endomysium and perimysium, but they were minimal in the skin. There were moderate variations in muscle fiber size. Some muscle fibers were atrophic. A scatter of necrotic muscle fibers was seen. The myositis, which is frequently observed in EF, may explain the EMG findings in this patient, as myotonic discharges may be seen in a number of acquired myopathic disorders, including myositis.1Also, certain drugs (eg, statins) can cause myotonic discharges.1The clinical characteristics, laboratory findings, and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of EF. The etiology and exact incidence of EF remain unknown. A variety of etiological factors have been proposed, such as strenuous exercise or trauma preceding disease onset.8To our knowledge, no randomized trials have evaluated therapies for EF. Usually, treatment is started with systemic glucocorticoids at doses equivalent to prednisone, 0.5 to 1 mg/kg per day.8Concomitant immunosuppressants (eg, methotrexate) are used by some practitioners as the initial therapy or when patients are steroid resistant or refractory.8,9For this patient, prednisone and cyclophosphamide were prescribed. Nine months later, his joint mobility was improved. Diagnosing EF is challenging because of its rarity. Bilaterally limited mobility of joints, cutaneous manifestations (eg, groove sign and orange peel appearance), and peripheral eosinophilia are useful clues to the diagnosis of EF.

scenario: A 62-year-old female presented with a generalized vesiculobullous rash of 4 months’ duration. The rash was insidious in onset and pruritic in nature. It started over the lips and gradually progressed to involve the oral mucosa and skin of the whole body. The patient also reported dry cough, dysuria, and tenesmus for a similar duration. Skin biopsy was suggestive of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Computed tomography scan performed for diagnostic evaluation showed a mass in the mesentery. Biopsy from the mass indicated follicular lymphoma.18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was next performed for the staging of lymphoma. Maximum intensity projection image (Figure 1A) showed heterogeneous uptake of18F-FDG in the skin of the visualized body. There was a distinctive visualization of almost the entire facial contour of the patient secondary to inflammation of the facial skin and the mucosa of the conjunctiva, nasal cavity, lips, and oral cavity (Figure 1B).18F-FDG uptake was also noticed along the mucosa of the esophagus, stomach, and intestines. The mesenteric mass showed low-intensity18F-FDG uptake. The patient started taking corticosteroid and cyclophosphamide-based prephase chemotherapy due to poor general condition. The clinical course was complicated by lower respiratory tract infection, which progressed to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction, and the patient died due to infective complications.
explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

scenario: A woman in her 60s was diagnosed with high-grade leiomyosarcoma of the uterus in 2017 for which she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. In 2020, she relapsed in the liver and spine. In November 2020, she underwent posterior lateral stabilization of C7-T4 for a T2 vertebral body metastasis causing cord compression, followed by postoperative stereotactic body radiation therapy to T2 to T3 (35 Gy/5 fractions) in January 2021. In February 2021, she received palliative radiation therapy (20 Gy/5 fractions) to T9 to T12 for a T11 vertebral body metastasis with epidural extension. From January to August 2021, she was treated with gemcitabine, and in September 2021, she received her first dose of liposomal doxorubicin. Two weeks later, she developed progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness, pain, weakness, and imbalance, prompting emergent evaluation. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings demonstrated extensive spinal cord edema extending from T2 to the conus and a posterior ring-enhancing intramedullary lesion at T9 to T10 without any mass effect (Figure 1). Because the intramedullary lesion appeared atypical for malignant disease given the lack of mass effect, she was prescribed high-dose steroids while further workup was pursued. Lumbar puncture showed no malignant cells. Positron emission tomographic-computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan demonstrated multifocal intensely F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease, but only mild uptake from T9 to T12 and no definitive FDG-avidity at the intramedullary lesion. Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.

options.B: Radiation recall myelopathy: continue steroids, discontinue doxorubicin
options.C: Radiation necrosis: continue steroids, add bevacizumab
options.D: Spinal cord infarct: underlying cause workup, supportive care
