scenario: A 28-year-old man presented to our hospital complaining of a bulge on the left side of his neck and severe stabbing pain during swallowing. The patient reported having experienced a left-side neck contusion 1 year prior with subsequent persistent pain, which the next day, developed into swelling and subcutaneous bleeding. These gradually improved over time; however, 2 weeks after the injury, he started experiencing a left cervical bulge and intense stabbing pain during swallowing. Despite having undergone various pharmacologic interventions at multiple medical facilities, these symptoms remained entirely unchanged. When the patient presented to our hospital, his vital signs were within normal ranges and blood tests revealed no abnormal findings. Symptomatically quiescent at rest, he reported substantial pain and swelling localized to the left sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and omohyoid (OH) muscles only during swallowing, accompanied by intense pain. Neck ultrasonography imaging was performed, which identified abnormal movement of the left OH toward the anterointernal direction during swallowing. Laryngoscopy and barium swallow testing showed no abnormalities. These findings were suggestive of posttraumatic scarring or neuritis; therefore, the patient was treated with ultrasonography-guided local triamcinolone injections around the bulging area and neuropathic pain medications; however, no improvement was noted. Hence, we performed swallowing dynamic computed tomography (SD-CT) to assess the dynamic structural changes during swallowing. SD-CT can reveal moving structures during swallowing by creating a dynamic-volume dataset.1,2The findings of SD-CT imaging at rest and during swallowing are shown inFigure 1and theVideo, A.
explanation: Given the findings of the reconstructed SD-CT imaging showing that the position of the intermediate tendon of the OH moved from a deep to a superficial position during swallowing and that it pushed the SCM up from below (Figure 2;Video), we diagnosed the patient with omohyoid muscle syndrome (OMS). Fifteen units of botulinum toxin type A (BTX) were injected into the OH for abnormal muscle contraction. After 1 week, the neck bulge and pain on swallowing were markedly improved; however, 3 months later, the bulging of the left side of the neck during swallowing and its associated symptoms reappeared. Injections of 20 units of BTX are currently being administered to the patient, as needed, for symptom management. OMS is a rare condition characterized by a lateral neck bulge that appears during swallowing and disappears at rest. Patients with OMS are asymptomatic at rest, and the symptoms, such as tenderness, discomfort, and limited cervical extension in the lateral neck, appear only during swallowing. The mechanisms of OMS include abnormal motion due to injury or loosening of the OH intermediate tendon and muscle fiber degeneration.1,2OMS is diagnosed on the basis of clinical presentation and diagnostic tests. Real-time ultrasonography imaging is a key diagnostic tool because it can demonstrate anterolateral displacement of the SCM by a thickened omohyoid muscle during swallowing.3,4Treatments for OMS include local injections of BTX or surgical treatment (OH resection by endoscopic or external approaches), with no symptom recurrence after surgery.5,6 The differential diagnoses for OMS include cervical chyloma, pseudoaneurysm, and traumatic cervical cystic hygroma. Cervical chyloma is an infrequent pseudocystic structure, which arises from the thoracic duct or its tributaries after a neck trauma or surgery, especially on the left side. CT scans and ultrasonography findings can confirm the cystic structure.7Pseudoaneurysms in the neck can occur due to various reasons, including trauma, iatrogenic injury during surgery, or radiation therapy, that can be associated with various symptoms, such as pain, dysphagia, hoarseness, or neurological deficits. A combination of imaging studies, including ultrasonography and CT angiography, is useful in its diagnosis.8Traumatic cervical cystic hygroma is a rare condition characterized by benign, painless, and soft swelling associated with lymphatic system malformations. It commonly presents in children 2 years or younger but can occur in older adults (60 years and older) in association with infection or trauma.9These conditions differ somewhat from OMS in terms of imaging findings and symptoms. In the present case, SD-CT revealed abnormal lateral movement of the OH during swallowing, suggesting some impairment of the intermediate tendon of the OH. Traumatic injury to the intermediate tendon can cause OH contraction during swallowing, which pushes up and compresses the SCM from the inside, forming a left cervical bulge. SD-CT was very useful in the diagnosis of OMS because it enabled us to observe the contraction of the entire OH, including the intermediate tendon, during swallowing. Four-dimensional evaluation by ultrasonography has been applied in the fetus and the heart,10but is currently not suitable for evaluation of neck musculature in terms of resolution and image evaluation range. Although pain is not common in OMS, the pain in this patient is likely associated with abnormal posttraumatic nerve regeneration. The patient reported less pain after the BTX injection; thus, BTX may be contributing to relief of pain and neck swelling during swallowing, likely by inhibiting OH movement during swallowing. Additional BTX treatment will be considered as needed; however, dosage and administration intervals should be adjusted according to the patient’s condition. Surgical treatment, such as partial left OH resection, is another option.

scenario: A large oral mass was noted at time of delivery in a female neonate at gestational age of 39 weeks. Primary symptom was difficulty feeding without notable respiratory distress. Prenatal history included maternal herpes simplex virus, well controlled with valacyclovir. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the neck with and without contrast was obtained showing a 3-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the posterior aspect of the tongue, abutting the inferior surface of the uvula with mild T1 hypointensity. On examination, a tan lobulated-appearing mass was noted occupying nearly all of the oral cavity and was adherent to the tongue posteriorly. No connection was noted to soft or hard palate, buccal mucosa, tonsillar fossae, or alveolar ridges. Surgical excision was performed on day 6 of life. The mass was noted to be attached just anteriorly to the dorsal lingual papillae with a wide base and was excised from the underlying tongue using cautery along with a cuff of lingual tissue (Figure 1). Direct laryngoscopy after removal of the mass revealed a grade I view with no other lesions present. Primary suture closure was accomplished without difficulty. The final specimen measured 3.5 cm anterior to posterior, 2.3 cm medial to lateral, and 1.1 cm in average thickness. The internal tissue was yellow-tan, fatty, and interdigitating with the underlying musculature.
explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

scenario: A 64-year-old woman with a history of hyperlipidemia, hypertension, HIV infection, coronary artery disease, and squamous cell carcinoma of the left mandible treated with composite resection, left neck dissection, and fibula free flap (FFF) reconstruction followed by postoperative radiotherapy presented with sharp, shooting left neck pain. Beginning 5 months after her reconstruction, the patient reported point tenderness on the left jaw, facial swelling, and electric pain with severity of 7 out of 10 in the left neck that occurred with talking or eating. Her postoperative course was complicated by osteoradionecrosis post-tracheostomy, plate removal, and left segmental mandibulectomy. She received regular physical therapy and lymphedema therapy and was seen by Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, who treated her with onabotulinum toxin A injections; neither provided significant resolution of her symptoms. Review of a computed tomography scan of the head and neck (Figure 1) performed on follow-up 5 years after initial reconstruction demonstrated a long, hyperdense structure in the left submental, submandibular region with accompanying soft-tissue thickening. On further review of prior imaging, this calcification appeared as a new finding in various scans dating back to 5 months after FFF reconstruction compared with preoperative imaging. There was no fluorodeoxyglucose avidity in the area of question on multiple positron emission tomography scans done during this follow-up window.

options.D: Ossification of the free flap pedicle

answer: Ossification of the free flap pedicle
explanation: D. Ossification of the free flap pedicle A painful neck mass is most worrisome for recurrence during surveillance of head and neck cancer.1,2Though traumatic neuroma or chronic postoperative pain is possible,3ossification of the FFF pedicle is the correct diagnosis for the following reasons. First, the lesion was stable over 5 years, with lack of fluorodeoxyglucose avidity on positron emission tomography, making recurrence less likely. Second, despite standard-of-care palliation techniques, her symptoms were recalcitrant. Third, the linear radiopacity located in the submental triangle, where the pedicle often courses, makes ossification more likely than a neuroma. The FFF is the standard for oromandibular reconstruction because of its high success rate and low donor-site morbidity.2A rare complication is pedicle ossification. Often asymptomatic, it may present as a firm, tender neck mass with trismus and pain with mastication and ipsilateral neck rotation.4,5Diagnostic imaging including computed tomography or panoramic radiographs can confirm this finding. Most commonly, pedicle ossification is detected incidentally on surveillance imaging.4The true incidence is unknown, with reports ranging from 4% to 65%; surprisingly, only 2.5% present symptomatically.4,6Ossification is more common in younger patients and those not receiving high-dose adjuvant radiotherapy.4 The pathogenesis remains unclear, but multiple theories describe pedicle ossification. The predominant theory implicates osteogenic proliferation of the periosteum along the vasculature.7During harvest, a cuff of muscle remains attached to the fibula alongside the peroneal vessels to preserve periosteal blood supply. Osteotomies are made to match the ablative geometry, leaving the periosteum and muscle along the pedicle, which atrophies and disappears over time.2However, under the stimulus of osteoinductive molecules, bone formation can occur from the periosteum and travel along the pedicle.2The osteogenic potential depends on local factors, including mechanical stress and proliferative stimuli.8Stretching of the periosteum during speech and mastication may be a key stimulus for osteogenesis.5In a rabbit model, costal periosteum has been shown to regenerate bony defects in the tibia within 6 weeks.9 Other theories include fracture repair, blood flow, local mechanics, and hormonal influence. The fracture repair theory describes osteoprogenitor recruitment in areas between recipient and donor osteotomy sites, which behave like a fracture. Blood flow theory, which relies on the interaction of stem cells and bone morphogenetic protein, asserts that higher perfusion in the leg compared with cervicofacial areas causes enhanced perfusion surrounding the pedicle after inset, leading to osteogenic stimulus and bone formation.2The local mechanical theory likens ossification to callus formation from masticatory stress, inducing bone morphogenetic protein signaling.2Some studies describe that the hormonal microenvironment (eg, high concentrations of estrogen and doses of dexamethasone) has been shown to increase osteogenic capacity.5However, this is disputed by some reports demonstrating a higher incidence of ossification in men or no statistical difference among sexes.6,8 Conservative therapy includes oral physiotherapy for 6 months after surgery.5Surgical excision (Figure 2) is recommended for functional or debilitating deficits and is considered safe given the natural history of pathogenesis. By the time of symptom manifestation, the flap has fully incorporated with adequate collateral circulation, permitting low-risk, outpatient surgery.4,5,7In the present patient’s case, her symptoms were refractory to nonsurgical therapy; therefore, excision of the ossified pedicle was undertaken. Though her neck discomfort resolved, her postoperative course was complicated by orocutaneous fistula, worsening osteoradionecrosis, and superinfection requiring hospitalization and tracheostomy. To minimize ossification, multiple studies advocate for a modified FFF harvest with additional dissection of periosteum along the pedicle and awareness of inset approaches to reduce mechanical stress from mastication.2,5Contradictory reports claim that there is no increased risk of flap loss with modified harvests, while others assert that the risk of vessel injury and flap compromise outweigh the low percentage of symptomatic cases.2,5,7

scenario: A 6-month-old girl presented to the emergency department for evaluation of fever and was noted to have mild inspiratory stridor. Her parents stated that her stridor began acutely at 4 months of age without any inciting illness or event. The stridor was worse with agitation but was without positional exacerbation. The family reported that the stridor had remained stable since onset. Her parents noted mild dysphagia but denied shortness of breath, cyanosis, or apnea. Laboratory test results revealed acute COVID-19 infection. Physical examination was unremarkable other than mild inspiratory stridor. Findings from bedside flexible laryngoscopy revealed intact vocal fold motion bilaterally with glottic competence. No supraglottic or glottic masses were identified. Anterior-posterior neck and chest radiography demonstrated narrowing and tortuosity of the trachea with displacement to the right proximal to the thoracic inlet and diffuse patchy heterogenous airspace opacities (Figure, A). Subsequent neck ultrasonography and computed tomography scan demonstrated a 3.2 × 2.0-cm low-density lesion abutting the trachea and hypopharynx at the level of thoracic inlet, with rightward displacement of the trachea and larynx (Figure, B-D). Operative laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and esophagoscopy revealed extrinsic compression of the trachea, right mainstem bronchus, and esophagus with rightward deviation of the trachea and esophagus. No mucosal tract was identified.
explanation: Foregut duplication cysts originate from persistent heterotopic rests of foregut-derived epithelium. Traditional diagnostic criteria include (1) attachment to some portion of the foregut, (2) the presence of an outer smooth muscle layer, and (3) an epithelial lining consistent with some portion of the foregut.1These cysts contain epithelial and mesenchymal elements related to the organ of origin. Accordingly, foregut duplication cysts are subclassified as bronchogenic cysts, esophageal duplication cysts, or enteric duplication cysts, depending on the epithelium.2,3Bronchogenic cysts are lined with ciliated respiratory epithelium, which may demonstrate squamous metaplasia and seromucinous glands, with underlying smooth muscle and hyaline cartilage resembling a bronchus. These are the most common, comprising more than 50% of mediastinal cysts.2Esophageal duplication cysts arise within the esophageal wall and are lined with squamous or respiratory-type epithelium and contain smooth or striated muscle reminiscent of the esophagus. Enteric duplication cysts are less commonly connected to the esophagus, but may be closely associated with vertebrae, and are lined with gastric or intestinal mucosa with an overlying muscle layer.3Of note, the cysts often demonstrate mixed mucosal types and may not represent the typical mucosa found at the anatomic level of the cyst.3In the described case, pathologic findings demonstrated mixed squamous and ciliated respiratory epithelium with stroma containing both smooth and skeletal muscle and benign mucosal glands, most consistent with bronchogenic duplication cyst. The pathogenesis of foregut duplication cyst development is unclear; however, the predominant theory of development is that the foregut fails to detach from the notochord at the appropriate time point in embryogenesis, as proposed by Veeneklaas in 19524and supported by animal studies from Qi et al.1Alternatively, the split notochord theory suggests that abnormal adherence of endoderm to the neural tube ectoderm could lead to herniation through the notochord, causing a posterior neuroenteric fistula.1 Foregut duplication cysts can present from the mouth to the anus; however, presentation in the head and neck is uncommon compared with the thorax or abdomen.5Within the head and neck, the cysts most commonly present as tongue lesions, with very few reported cases involving the pharynx or neck.2,5-9 Clinically, hypopharyngeal or neck foregut duplication cysts may be asymptomatic or present with airway obstruction or dysphagia.2,5These symptoms may present on a spectrum from respiratory compromise in the neonatal period requiring urgent intervention6-9to progressive stridor and dysphagia, as seen in the present patient.2 The differential diagnosis for foregut duplication cysts of the neck is broad. For patients presenting with airway obstruction in infancy, laryngeal cyst, thyroglossal duct cyst, cystic hygroma, hemangioma, and lymphoma must be considered.7,9For cases in which the cystic nature of the mass has been identified on imaging, the differential diagnosis includes laryngeal cyst, thyroglossal duct cyst, lymphatic or venous malformation, dermoid or epidermoid cyst, branchial cleft cyst, teratoma, and mucocele.2 Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are helpful in localizing and further evaluating the lesion, as well as for preoperative planning.2,5-8A smooth round or oval nonenhancing mass in a characteristic location can be highly suggestive of a foregut duplication cyst; however, it can be difficult to distinguish from lymphatic malformation owing to similar characteristics of internal contents.10Laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and esophagoscopy may be useful depending on the location of the cyst and may also serve to rule out other causes of cystic neck masses. However, as in the present patient, foregut duplication cysts of the neck, including esophageal duplication cysts, will likely present with extrinsic compression, and endoscopy may not narrow the differential further.2,5Importantly, definitive diagnosis is histopathologic.2,3,5 Management may consist of observation, aspiration, or surgical resection. While foregut duplication cysts are benign lesions, surgical resection is the treatment of choice.7,9First, histopathologic diagnosis is required for definitive diagnosis. In the event of respiratory compromise, aspiration may be considered in the short term; however, surgical resection is eventually required owing to high rates of recurrence after aspiration alone.2,5,9There are also risks of bleeding secondary to formation of peptic ulcers within cyst gastric mucosa and of sinus formation with active mucous secretion.2In the present case, the patient underwent surgical resection of the mass without evidence of recurrence after 8 months.

scenario: A 76-year-old Armenian man presented to the emergency department with a 6-week history of globus sensation and muffled voice and acute onset frank hemoptysis. He denied odynophagia, dysphagia, or dyspnea. He had a medical history of coronary artery disease with recent drug-eluting stent placement requiring use of clopidogrel and aspirin as well as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with fluticasone propionate/salmeterol inhaler for more than 20 years. The patient had no prior history of immunosuppression or organ transplant, and results of his HIV test were negative. He had no significant history of tobacco or alcohol use. Head and neck examination findings were notable for a small, purple, and painless nodule behind the left pinna. Laryngoscopy revealed a large mobile, multilobulated, broadly pedunculated mass that was friable and oozing on the lingual surface of the epiglottis (Figure 1A). Contrasted computed tomography of the neck and chest demonstrated a large lobulated enhancing soft tissue mass on the epiglottis measuring 3.5 × 2.3 × 1.6 cm without any suspicious lymphadenopathy, lung nodules, or any other masses (Figure 1B). There were no other abnormalities in the oropharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx. Operative direct laryngoscopy and debulking biopsies were performed. Bleeding was controlled with oxymetazoline and selective cauterization.
explanation: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a vascular neoplasm originating from endothelial cells of blood and lymphatic vessels infected with human herpes virus type 8 (HHV-8). The exact mechanism of HHV-8–mediated oncogenesis is not fully understood.1KS lesions usually appear as cutaneous painless violaceous macules that progress into indurated plaques and nodules with possible mucosal and visceral involvement. There are 4 variants of KS: classic (Mediterranean), endemic (African), iatrogenic (immunosuppressed/transplant related), and epidemic (HIV/AIDS associated). Classic KS is traditionally indolent, presenting in the lower extremities of elderly men of Mediterranean or eastern European descent. Classic KS may also be a sign of a secondary malignant neoplasm.2Lesions may appear in the head and neck, especially the oropharynx and lymph nodes. Although an uncommon cause of laryngeal mass, KS poses a life-threatening risk of airway obstruction if not identified and managed promptly3and thus should be considered in the differential diagnosis of a patient with hemoptysis and a laryngeal mass. Diagnostic features include a violaceous pedunculated mass on laryngoscopy with narrow-band imaging confirming high vascularity. Imaging findings are nonspecific, often describing an enhancing mass affecting 1 or more laryngeal subsites. Tissue biopsy is diagnostic with hallmark features of slitlike vascular spaces formed by spindled cells and immunohistochemistry positive for HHV-8, CD34, and CD31.2There is currently no guideline in the management of KS in the larynx, but a recent systematic review suggests its management and prognosis depend on the variant, depth of invasion, and involvement of surrounding structures.3Classic KS is treated with larynx-sparing surgical excision or radiotherapy with complete resolution of disease, whereas epidemic KS was typically treated with chemotherapy and had poor outcomes. In this case, the patient most likely has classic KS. A shared decision was made to perform urgent operative direct laryngoscopy and excisional biopsies. The patient was easily mask ventilated but was difficult to intubate due to poor visualization from the large mobile and oozing tumor, and thus a Dedo laryngoscope was used to intubate. A Lindholm laryngoscopy was used to examine the airway followed by debulking biopsies of the entire lingual epiglottic mass off the cartilage itself using a combination of straight and up-biting cups and alligator forceps. Histopathology revealed spindle-shaped cells arranged in a slitlike pattern and positive immunohistochemical staining for CD34 and HHV-8 consistent with KS (Figure 2). The patient elected for watchful waiting given localized disease. After 3 months, he returned with reported increased cutaneous lesions affecting his ear, lower extremities and trunk as well as globus sensation. Laryngoscopy showed many lesions on his larynx, including a 1.5-cm pedunculated mass on the left arytenoid that partially obstructs airflow with inspiration and smaller lesions on the right posterior arytenoid, right ventricle, and right laryngeal surface of the epiglottis. Excisional biopsy of the left arytenoid mass confirmed KS. He did well after 8 cycles of doxorubicin but relapsed 2 years later with cutaneous lesions but none involving the larynx on laryngoscopy. Doxorubicin was restarted with good success. This case demonstrated laryngoscopy and immunohistopathology findings of KS, an uncommon cause for a supraglottic and laryngeal mass.

scenario: A 16-year-old male with a history of mild seasonal allergies presented with right-sided congestion, thick discolored nasal drainage, facial pain/pressure, anosmia, and intermittent epistaxis for approximately 1 year. Nasal endoscopy revealed moderate global deviation of the septum to the left. On the right, thick mucus and crusting anterior to the middle turbinate was seen, completely occluding the nasal cavity. Physical examination was otherwise normal. Magnetic resonance imaging showed a heterogeneous, expansile mass measuring 6 (anteroposterior) × 3.1 (transverse) × 5 (craniocaudal) cm within the right nasal cavity extending to the nasopharynx, with obliteration of the nasopharyngeal airway and anteroinferior displacement of the soft palate (Figure, B). The adjacent sinuses had drainage obstruction. Biopsy results showed fragments of necrotic and fibrinous debris with acute inflammatory exudate and bacterial colonies. Findings during surgery included a fibrous expansile mass filling the right nasal cavity and bowing the septum to the left. It crossed the midline to fill the nasopharynx and extended inferiorly toward the oropharynx. The mass was noted to originate at the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus. Pathologic evaluation showed fragments of polypoidal mucosa with edematous stroma, numerous ectatic vascular channels, and a sprinkling of inflammatory cells (Figure, A). The surface epithelium was largely ulcerated, covered with fibrinous and inflammatory debris and bacterial colonies. Immunostaining showed CD31 and CD34 positivity. Stromal cells did not have β-catenin present. Elastic stain results showed scant elastic fibers in the vascular proliferation.
explanation: Of the 5 histological subtypes of sinonasal polyps (edematous, glandular, fibrous, cystic, and angiomatous or angiectatic), angiomatous nasal polyps (ANPs) make up about 4% to 5% of these sinonasal lesions.1Sinonasal polyps may present with nasal obstruction, facial pain or pressure, snoring, anosmia, epistaxis, and nasal drainage.2Some reports of ANPs describe a foul odor associated with the lesions, raising concern for bacterial, fungal, or malignant processes.3These presenting symptoms, however, are nonspecific, and additional workup must be completed to assess for other causes, such as inverted papilloma (IP), sinonasal tract angiofibroma (STA), and lobular capillary hemangioma (LCH). On computed tomography, ANPs typically present as a heterogenous density with minimal enhancement at the lesion’s edges and accompanying bony changes.4When visualized on magnetic resonance imaging, ANPs display heterogeneous isointense signal intensity on T1-weighted images and a hypointense peripheral rim on T2-weighted images.5IPs may have similar imaging appearance and display hypointense T1 signal with isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted image; contrast enhancement is in a convoluted cerebriform pattern.6Imaging of LCHs often show bone destruction and evidence of phleboliths.7STAs typically demonstrate heterogenous signal intensity on T1-weighted images and may be either high intensity or isointensity predominant on T2-weighted images.8Internal flow voids and intense enhancement are also seen in the majority of STAs, as well as LCHs.7In STAs, involvement of the sphenopalatine foramen/pterygopalatine fossa is often present,8which is not seen in ANPs. Location of origin is another factor that may differentiate these tumors. ANPs typically originate from the maxillary sinus and may spread to the choana.4LCHs most commonly originate from the anterior nasal septum, while STAs originate from the sphenopalatine foramen region along the posterior nasal cavity.7Alternatively, IPs usually arise from the lateral nasal wall or the paranasal sinuses. Imaging findings for this patient reflect ANP, with a large heterogeneous expansile mass extending from the right nasal cavity to the nasopharynx and into the posterior aspect of the maxillary sinus, with mass effect and mild resorption of the surrounding bones. When examined via light microscopy, ANPs often have an ulcerated roof and areas lined by respiratory epithelium, which may show squamous metaplasia.2ANPs also show scattered atypical pleomorphic spindle cells in the stroma, a paucity of inflammatory infiltrate, and abundant amorphous, Congo red–negative material.1ANPs are characterized by a high degree of vascular proliferation and ectasia; as such, these blood vessels may be subject to compression leading to infarction.3Given the highly vascularized and potentially necrotic nature of ANPs, it is understandable that these polyps may present with diagnostic difficulty due to potential confusion with other vascular tumors. Fully developed LCHs typically display lobules of back-to-back capillaries, with endothelial cells divided by fibrous or myxoid septa.9STAs, on the other hand, demonstrate a dense stromal component with numerous fibroblasts and have varying levels of vessel density. Immunohistochemical stains are also helpful in differentiating STAs from other tumors and will be positive for β-catenin, androgen receptor, estrogen receptor β, and prostate-specific antigen.7IPs are characterized histologically by an inverted appearance due to thickened epithelium enclosed by basement membrane, along with transmigrating intraepithelial neutrophilic inflammation.6The pathology and immunohistochemistry findings, as outlined in this case, align with ANP. The standard treatment for ANPs is resection via endoscopic approach. This treatment allows for symptom relief and a definitive pathologic characterization. Removal of the site of origin of these polyps is crucial for preventing recurrence. The present patient underwent successful endoscopic resection and followed up regularly outpatient after surgery. The patient’s presenting symptoms have resolved, and there was no evidence of recurrence at 6 months.

scenario: An 11-year-old girl with no significant medical history was referred to the pediatric otolaryngology department for a painless, left-sided neck mass that had been slowly enlarging for 8 months. On examination, there was an easily palpable 3-cm firm, fixed, well-circumscribed left supraclavicular mass without overlying skin changes or cutaneous involvement. She had no other masses, cervical lymphadenopathy, or systemic symptoms. In workup for this mass, she initially underwent ultrasound imaging, which demonstrated a hypoechoic mass. Findings from fine-needle aspiration and core-needle biopsy were inconclusive, demonstrating histiocytes. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a well-circumscribed mass of mainly soft tissue density with contrast enhancement (Figure 1). Given persistence of the lesion, and inconclusive biopsies, the decision was made to pursue surgical excision. In the operating room, a well-defined 5.5-cm left level V mass was excised. The mass was found to attach deep to the middle scalene and was fed by several unnamed vessels; however, there was no involvement of the clavicle. Pathology confirmed complete excision of a well-circumscribed lesion with peripheral casing of bone, cyst-like spaces filled with serous fluid, walls of spindle-shaped fibroblasts, osteoclast-type giant cells, thin trabeculae of woven bone surfaced with osteoblasts, and scattered macrophages. There was local infiltration into surrounding skeletal muscle, but no atypical mitoses or pleomorphic cells were identified. The lesion was positive forUSP6locus rearrangement (17p13.2) on florescence in situ hybridization.
explanation: C. Soft tissue aneurysmal bone cyst The gross and microscopic findings were characteristic of a soft tissue (extraosseous) aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) withUSP6locus rearrangement, confirming the diagnosis (Figure 2). Aneurysmal bone cysts are benign but locally aggressive tumors most commonly found in association with the long bones and spines of children and young adults.1,2Extraosseous or soft tissue ABCs pathologically and genetically resemble those associated with bone but lack a bony attachment.2Soft tissue ABCs are a rare phenomenon with approximately 40 cases reported in the literature.3Extraosseous ABCs were first described in 1972 by Salm and Sissons as soft tissue lesions with identical histopathological findings as ABCs.4Aneurysmal bone cysts are classically described as bony-shelled, blood-filled cysts with fibrous septa, which contain giant cells, woven bone, fibroblasts, and histiocytes.5-7In 1999, Dal Cin et al described chromosomal rearrangement of 17p13 in all ABCs, including those associated only with soft tissue, confirming similar neoplastic pathogenesis.8Furthermore,USP6locus rearrangement has been determined to be sensitive for ABCs in a more recent study by Li et al.9Magnetic resonance imaging is identical to osseous ABCs, demonstrating an expansile lesion, T2-weighted intense, with strong contrast enhancement and fluid levels.2,6,7,10These lesions tend to occur within the first 2 decades of life, and of cases reported there is no sex predominance.2,10Aneurysmal bone cysts, including the soft tissue variety, are difficult to diagnose given their rarity and similar presentation, clinically and radiographically, to other more common tumors such as giant cell tumors, extraskeletal osteosarcomas, ossifying fibromyxoid tumors, and myositis ossificans.2,3,6,7 Extraosseous ABCs are rare in the head and neck. In 1993, Petrik et al described a 3-cm left common carotid mass in a 7-year-old boy, excised completely with no intracranial or bony component.4Of other reported cases, most have occurred within the soft tissue of the limbs.2,4Definitive treatment for these tumors, regardless of anatomical site, is complete surgical excision.2-7Recurrence risk is reported as low in the literature, with a 2019 review citing 5% after incomplete excision.3 The present case represents a classic presentation of a soft tissue ABC of the head and neck. Imaging and pathology represent the characteristic findings of this entity, and the diagnosis was able to be confirmed with gene rearrangement. The patient did well with surgical excision and has returned to normal activities with no concern for recurrence. Soft tissue ABCs should be considered on the differential for any slowly enlarging mass of the head and neck in the pediatric population.

scenario: A woman in her early 50s presented with a neck mass, incidentally discovered during evaluation of recurrent headaches. She reported mild solid food dysphagia but was otherwise asymptomatic. Physical examination revealed fullness in the location of the left thyroid lobe. Flexible laryngoscopy showed normal vocal fold movement and laboratory findings were within normal limits. Ultrasonography revealed a 2.4-cm hypoechoic nodule posterior to the left thyroid lobe, with suggestion of a feeding vessel (Figure 1). An ultrasonography-guided fine-needle aspiration for the presumed thyroid nodule was performed, but definitive characterization was not possible with the limited material obtained. Therefore, a 20-gauge core biopsy was attempted but was aborted due to patient discomfort. Because of the unclear diagnosis, she was scheduled for a left thyroid lobectomy with excision of the mass. Postoperatively, she experienced resolution of her dysphagia and vocal fold function was normal.
explanation: Granular cell tumors (GCTs) are rare soft-tissue neoplasms with neuroectodermal differentiation.1Most GCTs are benign and incidentally found, and previous reports indicate that only 1% to 2% are malignant.1They occur in soft tissues throughout the entire body, most commonly in the skin, tongue, subcutaneous tissue, and skeletal muscle but also occur in the nervous system, respiratory tract, and all segments of the gastrointestinal tract.1Of all GCTs, approximately half appear in the head and neck and approximately 5% to 11% occur in the gastrointestinal tract.2,3Of the latter, 65% of esophageal GCTs are located in the distal esophagus, 20% in the middle, and 15% in the proximal esophagus.3 There is a female preponderance (75%) with a mean age of 41 years.3Dysphagia and weight loss are the most common presenting symptoms, but the majority are asymptomatic.3,4The average tumor size on presentation in the cervical region is 2.4 cm, with symptomatic tumors being significantly larger than asymptomatic lesions.4 GCTs are characterized histologically by large cells with abundant granular cytoplasm, bland nuclei, and indistinct nucleoli.1,5S100 protein positivity by immunohistochemistry is typical of this tumor and periodic acid–Schiff with diastase staining highlights the granules within the cytoplasm.1,5Recommended treatment for GCTs has generally included complete excision of tumors, especially those greater than 1 cm, to prevent recurrence and reduce the possibility of malignant transformation, the latter estimated to occur in 1% to 2% of cases.1,6Although the growth rate of these tumors is not known due to its rarity, it should be recommended that these tumors be addressed early after diagnosis to prevent subsequent growth and potential additional morbidity related to more extensive esophageal resection and reconstruction.6 Owing to its rarity and low incidence, there is presently no consensus regarding appropriate esophageal GCT diagnostic testing, management, and surveillance.1,2,6It is important to note that the following characteristics are based on prior case series and studies, and a multidisciplinary approach is necessary for accurate diagnosis and management of esophageal GCTs.1,2On ultrasonography, they are often hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged.2Color Doppler can be used to distinguish between lymph nodes (hilar flow pattern) and parathyroid nodules (polar flow pattern).5Magnetic resonance imaging of GCTs reveals low T1 signal intensity, homogenous enhancement, and high T2 signal intensity. On computed tomography, they are solid and exhibit homogenous enhancement (can resemble squamous cell carcinoma).1,2Multiple prior studies have suggested the utility of endoscopic esophageal ultrasonography in the diagnosis and treatment of GCTs.2,3,6Typical endoscopic ultrasonography imaging characteristic of GCTs include hypoechoic, homogenous, and smooth-edged tumors restricted to deep mucosal and submucosal layers; however, there have been 2 cases reported with tumors invading the muscular layer, to our knowledge.2,6 In the case presented here (Figure 2), a firm mass was identified intraoperatively between the muscular and mucosal layers of the esophagus and deep to the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. The mass was also positioned deep to both parathyroid glands. The mass was removed with the left thyroid lobe while preserving the parathyroid glands and recurrent laryngeal nerve. The patient has been followed up with annual ultrasonography for 5 years since the surgery, with no evidence of residual or recurrent disease. GCTs of the head and neck are uncommon, and limited information is available regarding their imaging characteristics and preoperative cytologic features, particularly when involving the cervical esophagus.1,4It is important to consider GCTs in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses. Imaging (eg, ultrasonography) and cytologic evaluation of fine-needle aspiration specimens can be informative with an adequate specimen, but definitive diagnosis may require surgical resection.4,5

scenario: A 48-year old woman presented with a 4-week history of episodic headaches and light sensitivity. She reported falling on her head, which marked the onset of her headaches. Within 3 weeks, she noticed a painful, pulsating mass on the right side of her forehead, which she initially attributed to the fall. She also had a history of hypertension, which worsened the symptoms of headaches and the swelling of the mass. She denied experiencing fever, chills, night sweats, or any changes in her vision. The patient’s medical history was significant for diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and thyroid nodules that were previously biopsied as benign. At that point, her medication history included 4 months of semaglutide, along with metformin and losartan. She formerly smoked. The physical examination and imaging revealed a 2.5-cm mass/swelling on the right frontal calvarium (Figure 1). Imaging results were significant for thyromegaly, but no other sites of metastatic disease were observed in the chest, abdomen, or pelvis. The mass was biopsied, revealing a 1.6-cm right anterior calvarial lesion, which prompted a neurosurgery referral for further evaluation. She underwent resection of the right frontal calvarial mass and cranioplasty reconstruction.
explanation: C. Metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma The pathology report of the anterior calvarial lesion biopsy specimen revealed a follicle-forming tumor of thyroid origin that was consistent with metastatic follicular thyroid carcinoma, and the patient was subsequently referred for further thyroid evaluation. Although previous nodule biopsy specimens revealed benign cysts, recent computed tomography of the neck revealed partially calcified and heterogeneously enhancing nodules. Total thyroidectomy was completed, revealing a 5.6-cm thyroid tumor. Pathology results showed poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma (PDTC) arising from a background of follicular thyroid carcinoma and T3aN0M1 staging. PDTC is in the category of high-grade follicular, cell-derived nonanaplastic thyroid carcinoma, with a definition of neoplasm of thyroid follicular cells with high-grade features with mitotic count and tumor necrosis without anaplastic histology. In this case, resection specimen showed a solid growth pattern of follicular cells with multifocal capsular invasion and focal lymphatic invasion. Tumor nests demonstrated solid/trabecular architecture with minimal to no colloid (Figure 2A). There was no papillary architecture or papillary thyroid carcinoma nuclear feature identified in this case. Tumor cells were small to medium size, with round nuclei, indistinct nucleoli, and a lack of anaplasia. Occasional nuclei show convoluted and irregular contours. Large zonal necrosis and increased mitosis (10 per 2 mm2) were identified (Figure 2B). Per Turin and World Health Organization criteria, this lesion is categorized as poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma.1 In general, PDTC has more aggressive behavior, and prognosis is between well-differentiated follicular carcinoma (such as papillary thyroid carcinoma or follicular carcinoma) and anaplastic carcinoma.2PDTC shows a higher T and N stage and 5-year survival rate is between 50% to 70%. Specific molecular alterations unique for PDTC are not identified, and they generally harborBRAF V600EorRAS,NRAS, andTERTvariants. A 2023 study showed somatic variants of ABCA12,CLIP1, andATP13A3were significantly associated with a vascular invasion phenotype.3 More than 40 000 individuals receive a diagnosis of thyroid cancer each year in the US.4The second most prevalent type of thyroid cancer is follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC), which arises from the follicular cells responsible for producing iodine-containing thyroid hormones.5Distant metastases occur in approximately 10% to 15% of FTC cases, with the bones and lungs being the most common sites.6Secondary skull metastases originating from FTC are rare, comprising only 2% to 5% of all skeletal metastases from the thyroid.7These cases are more common in female patients, with headaches being the most frequently reported symptom.7 In rare cases, patients with metastatic FTC can present with progressively enlarging frontal skull masses. The masses are firm, pulsatile, and fixed to the skull, with some cases exhibiting mobility.8In many instances, patients remain asymptomatic apart from the noticeable swelling, leading to delayed diagnosis.8However, patients who present with concurrent neck masses may experience compressive symptoms, such as difficulty swallowing or breathing.9Headaches are commonly reported, particularly in cases of hypertension that exacerbates the episodic headaches as described in this article. Patients may also develop neurological symptoms, such as seizures and light sensitivity.9,10 In their systematic review of 20 patients with secondary skull analysis from FTC, Scalia et al7highlighted that FTC skull metastases predominantly affect women (mean age, 65.6 years). Some patients presented with isolated skull masses (most commonly in the anterior calvarium), while others had concurrent thyroid lesions. In cases in which FTC metastases progress, symptoms such as headaches became more prominent (70% of reported cases).7Despite the differences in presentation, the overall clinical pattern remains consistent: painless, slow-growing skull masses that may be accompanied with an enlarged thyroid gland. These findings emphasize the importance of timely imaging studies, referrals, and biopsies in diagnosing FTC metastases to confirm thyroid origin and implement proper treatment to ensure good patient outcomes.

scenario: A 2-month-old, full-term female presented with a left upper neck mass that was first noted at birth. Her parents reported no fevers, constitutional symptoms, or enlargement of the mass. On physical examination, there was a nontender 4-cm mass in the left submandibular region with no overlying skin changes. Ultrasonography results showed an avascular cystic structure with internal debris and a single thin septation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the neck soft tissue revealed a 3-cm low attenuation, nonenhancing, cystic-appearing mass that elevated the submandibular gland to the level of the parapharyngeal fat space with medial extension of the lesion into the tongue musculature. The walls were thin except for mildly thickened capsule along the posterior aspect of the lesion (Figure, A and B). Fluid that aspirated from the cyst was serous, and cytology showed mature and anucleate squamous cells with acute inflammation. The mass returned after 3 weeks. Further analysis 8 months after the initial CT via contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a large, multiseptated cystic structure (Figure, C); the capsule of the wall was mildly thickened and was contrast enhancing. At age 12 months, the mass was excised via neck dissection. A lateral component at the level of the sternocleidomastoid muscle was completely excised. An intraoperative rupture of the thin capsule caused some spillage of cystic contents that were milky white in some areas and mucinous in others.
explanation: Foregut duplication cysts are uncommon floor of the mouth masses that result from remnant embryological foregut structures. They often present as neck masses in otherwise healthy neonates and raise concern for swallowing difficulties and airway obstruction.1-3By definition, the cysts must have a smooth muscle layer, contain foregut-derived epithelium, and attach to a portion of the foregut.2-4Histologically, they contain multiple types of epithelium, including squamous, gastric, respiratory, and cuboidal.4Only 0.3% of foregut duplication cysts appear in the head and neck, and 60% of these cases involve the oral cavity.4Treatment includes observation, aspiration, and resection; recurrence is rare after complete resection of the mucosal lining.2-4 Preoperative imaging is recommended for suspected foregut duplication cysts and can aid in diagnosis.2Generally, the cysts are well-circumscribed and nonseptated, although occasional septations are possible, as seen in this patient.5Ultrasonography reveals a double-wall sign with an inner hyperechoic mucosa-submucosa layer and an outer hypoechoic, muscularis propria layer. Computed tomography shows a uniform cystic lesion with occasional septations and fluid-debris levels. On T2-weighted MRI, the cysts have uniformly high signals, whereas T1-weighted MRI shows variable intensity because of protein contents.3,5 Branchial cleft cysts constitute approximately 20% of all excised pediatric cervical masses, following the failure of pharyngobranchial ducts to entirely obliterate during fetal development.6They present as tender, inflammatory masses along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle much later in childhood than foregut duplication cysts.6,7Younger patients may present with fistulas between the cyst and external surface of the neck. On imaging, branchial cleft cysts are well-defined, thin-walled, and anechoic. Imaging with T2-weighted MRI shows a hyperintense cyst without wall enhancement. A pathognomonic finding on imaging is an extension of the cyst between the internal and external carotid arteries (beak sign), which was not seen in this patient.6Treatment is surgical excision.1 A ranula is a mucocele or pseudocyst that occurs because of ductal obstruction of the sublingual gland. Plunging ranulas invade the submandibular space through a mylohyoid defect.6,7They present as slow-growing, painless, submental masses; however, they rarely present before the second decade.6,7On ultrasonography, plunging ranulas appear anechoic and lobulated. Computed tomography shows unilocular, thin-walled cystic lesions. Similarly, T2-weighted MRI shows thin-walled cystic structures with high signals that are often accompanied by hyperintense tail-like extensions of the ranula from the submandibular into the sublingual space.6The association of the described lesion with the submandibular gland raised suspicion for a ranula; however, the presence of multiple septations proved inconsistent with this diagnosis. Treatment involves excision of the sublingual gland, as the ranula itself is nonsecreting.7 Lymphatic malformations of the submandibular space arise from connection failures of the lymphatic system. They present at birth or before age 2 years as soft, smooth, nontender, compressible masses.6,7The masses are further divided into macrocystic (>2 cm), microcystic (<2 cm), or mixed. Generally, imaging results reveal a multiloculated cyst with extension of the malformation into surrounding neurovascular structures. Ultrasonography shows intracystic debris with multiple septations. On CT, they appear as multicystic lesions of low attenuation. Contrast-enhanced MRI generally shows thin peripheral and septal enhancement.3While this patient did have a multiloculated cyst, the T1 single intensity, which was consistent with proteinaceous fluid, favored diagnosis of a foregut duplication cyst. After the patient’s surgery, pathology reports showed multiple cysts that were lined by squamous, ciliated bronchiolar-type, and flattened cuboidal epithelia that were associated with salivary and pancreatic glandular structures. Nodules containing pancreatic tissues with islets were present, which was consistent with a foregut duplication cyst. The mass was attached to the retromolar trigone mucosa, which also supported the diagnosis. Two months after surgery, the patient appeared well, with no evidence of mass recurrence or neck fullness.
